Adopted in the opening-day rules package by simple majority.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes the balance between leadership stability and member leverage, which constrains what any Speaker is able to schedule or negotiate.
rows.Current Status (Optional): The 2019 change removed the referral step; the one-member threshold has been adjusted between Congresses
rows.Concerns: The higher threshold has to be adopted in an opening-day rules package by the same majority whose members lowered it to one person in 2015 and 2023, and a future majority can lower it again the same way.
rows.Sources: Working Group Reform Options Package (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: No camera-free space exists where members of both parties talk
rows.Problem Description: Cross-party conversation has no informal venue near the floor, so the relationships that make negotiation possible form by accident or not at all.
rows.Solution Statement: Convert the Speaker's Lobby into a bipartisan members-only space
rows.Solution Description: Designate the Speaker's Lobby members-only, excluding press, lobbyists, and non-member staff, and reseat it through the Architect of the Capitol for small-group conversation, making it more attractive than the cloakrooms. The Speaker can act alone; a joint leadership statement makes it durable.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates the chance for relationships without touching the incentives that keep members apart, and the next Speaker can undo it.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #45. Informal cross-party relationships formed in a shared space build the trust members need to reach the bipartisan committee thresholds that a guaranteed regular-order procedure rewards with priority floor consideration.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
Proposed previously; the Senate has an equivalent room
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 30: Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Implementing text included in H.Res. 1331; need to identify space in the Capitol with close proximity to the House Floor that can be optimized for members gathering and collaborating in private and across party lines.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 7 (tracker Rec 30): Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Implementing text included in H.Res. 1331; need to identify space in the Capitol with close proximity to the House Floor that can be optimized for members gathering and collaborating in private and across party lines.
rows.Concerns: The Speaker can act alone, which means the next Speaker can also undo it alone, and a members-only lounge changes where people can talk without changing the primary incentives that keep members from wanting to.
rows.Sources:
Working Group Reform Options Package (April 2026)
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 7
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562/pdf/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562.pdf

rows.Problem Statement: Congress underfunds its own capacity
rows.Problem Description: Flat since the early 2000s, the legislative branch budget gives a growing share to the Capitol Visitor Center and Capitol Police as the executive branch it oversees grows enormously.
rows.Solution Statement: Targeted legislative branch capacity initiative
rows.Solution Description: Win a bipartisan leadership commitment to prioritize capacity in the next appropriations cycle, increases targeted to GAO, CBO, CRS, Legislative Counsel, committee funds, a restored Office of Technology Assessment, and member allowances for staff pay and casework technology, not across the board and excluding security.
rows.Horizon Justification: A single-cycle increase rebuilds capability while the budget's trajectory and the politics behind it stay put; the case recurs annually.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #118. Winning one bipartisan appropriations cycle proves capacity funding can succeed politically, and that coalition is what a formula tying legislative branch funding to a fixed share of spending needs to lock in permanently.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
Proposed for the next cycle
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 84 (tracker Rec 84): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: FY 2022 and 2023 Legislative Branch Appropriations bills increased budgets, allowing for more investment in policy staff; need to examine the potential for GAO to expand its role.
rows.Concerns: Excluding security from the increase leaves out the accounts growing fastest and most visible to leadership, and a single appropriations cycle does not change the budget trajectory that produced the flat funding in the first place.
rows.Sources:
Working Group Reform Options Package (April 2026)
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 84
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562/pdf/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562.pdf
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: Congress's budget does not scale with what it oversees
rows.Problem Description: The legislative branch has averaged around 0.15 percent of federal budget authority since 1976 and can be quietly starved relative to the government it appropriates for, since its own funding competes annually against every other priority.
rows.Solution Statement: Tie legislative branch funding to a fixed share of federal spending
rows.Solution Description: Establish by standalone legislation, or by a chamber rule setting a target sub-allocation, a floor for legislative branch appropriations as a fixed percentage of non-defense discretionary spending, indexed to a multi-year average and reviewed periodically. A related version funds oversight as a line item set as a percentage of the executive branch budgets being overseen.
rows.Horizon Justification: It removes Congress's capacity from the annual political decision that has eroded it, making the institution's own resourcing structural rather than discretionary.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed independently by multiple groups
rows.Concerns: A fixed floor still has to be carved out of a capped non-defense discretionary total, so it competes directly against every other protected account rather than adding new money to the pie.
rows.Sources:
Working Group Reform Options Package (April 2026)
Recoding America ModSub Submissions (2026)
Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Security spending masks the decline in congressional capacity
rows.Problem Description: Growth in Capitol Police, Visitor Center, and Architect of the Capitol funding sits in the same bill as staff, committee, and support agency accounts, so the legislative branch total looks stable while capacity accounts stagnate.
rows.Solution Statement: Separate security funding into its own line
rows.Solution Description: Split security accounts out of the legislative branch capacity accounts, either as distinct lines within the bill or as a separate measure, so the capacity argument can be made on its own terms and the two are not traded against each other.
rows.Horizon Justification: Reorganizing the presentation clarifies the argument without adding a dollar to either side, and the trade-off it exposes still has to be won.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #118. Splitting security spending into its own line isolates the capacity shortfall on its own terms, supplying the evidence needed to peg legislative branch funding to a fixed share of federal spending rather than negotiate it against security every year.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed
rows.Concerns: Splitting the presentation clarifies the capacity argument but does not move a dollar, and once security has its own line, cutting it becomes a more visible political target than folding it into the larger legislative branch total.
rows.Sources:
Working Group Reform Options Package (April 2026)
Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: No one has mapped how congressional capacity is organized
rows.Problem Description: Staffing structure, distribution of expertise, duplication across offices, and service orientation have never been assessed as a whole, so reform proposals are made without a picture of the current state.
rows.Solution Statement: Congressional capacity landscape analysis
rows.Solution Description: Commission a comprehensive assessment by a nonpartisan organization with organizational-assessment expertise, run separately for the House and Senate, producing restructuring options rather than diagnosis alone and running in parallel with the appropriations ask rather than delaying it.
rows.Horizon Justification: An assessment produces options that someone else must choose to act on, and the absence of an owner for those options is itself part of the problem being assessed.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #99. The commissioned landscape analysis supplies the organizational assessment and restructuring options that the Secretary General proposal explicitly builds from, converting a one-time diagnostic into the evidence base for a senior civil servant who owns implementation.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed
rows.Concerns: A landscape analysis produces restructuring options that only House and Senate leadership can choose to act on, and nothing here names who owns that choice, the same gap the assessment is meant to diagnose.
rows.Sources: Working Group Reform Options Package (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Committees lack expertise in their own subject matter
rows.Problem Description: Many committees have no professional technical staff in the areas they legislate on, and personal offices have none at all, so the expertise in any given hearing belongs to the witnesses.
rows.Solution Statement: Committee-housed technical experts offered as a shared service
rows.Solution Description: House technical experts at the committee level and make them available as a service to all offices, on a pay scale that permits recruiting from the executive branch and industry.
rows.Horizon Justification: It builds permanent subject matter capacity inside the institution and spreads it beyond the committee that hosts it, rather than borrowing expertise per project.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed
rows.Concerns: A committee that hosts the shared experts has an incentive to keep them working its own agenda first, so the service actually reaching other offices depends on norms rather than any structural guarantee.
rows.Sources: Working Group Reform Options Package (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Bipartisan House-passed bills die without Senate coordination
rows.Problem Description: Legislation that clears one chamber with bipartisan support restarts from zero in the other, and vetted bills start over again each Congress.
rows.Solution Statement: Bicameral coordination of bipartisan bills
rows.Solution Description: Convene a bicameral working group of leadership designees and committee staff to identify ten to twenty bipartisan bills eligible for coordination and flag them for prioritized consideration in the other chamber. Pair it with a House fast-track review process letting committees readvance bipartisan bills passed in a prior Congress.
rows.Horizon Justification: A coordination group depends entirely on leadership goodwill in both chambers and covers a handful of bills, leaving the underlying absence of any cross-chamber pathway intact.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #123. The ad hoc working group's practice of identifying and prioritizing bipartisan bills for cross-chamber action builds a working pipeline that a revitalized, rules-based conference process can resolve routinely, replacing leadership goodwill with standing procedure and trained staff.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed
rows.Concerns: The working group has no authority beyond leadership's willingness to prioritize the bills it flags, covers only ten to twenty bills a Congress, and leaves no standing mechanism for the ones that follow.
rows.Sources: Working Group Reform Options Package (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Almost no one knows how to run a conference committee
rows.Problem Description: The conference process has atrophied: rules are out of date and inconsistent between chambers, and few staff in either chamber have ever convened or run one, so differences get resolved in leadership negotiations instead.
rows.Solution Statement: Revitalize the conference committee process
rows.Solution Description: Review and amend conference rules in each chamber to standardize how conferences are convened, conferees appointed, and reports produced; train dedicated conference clerks in each chamber to hold the institutional knowledge; and build the committee infrastructure to make the process operable. Advanced through each chamber's rules package or a resolution directing the Clerk to publish standard procedures.
rows.Horizon Justification: Restoring a working conference process changes where bicameral differences are resolved, moving them from leadership offices back to the committees that wrote the bills.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Atrophied; conferences are now rare
rows.Concerns: Standardized rules and trained clerks do not compel leadership to use conference committees instead of the direct negotiations it currently controls, so the revived infrastructure can sit unused if leadership prefers keeping resolution power to itself.
rows.Sources: Working Group Reform Options Package (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: The debt ceiling creates a recurring crisis with no fiscal function
rows.Problem Description: The limit does not control spending already enacted, and each standoff threatens borrowing costs and economic stability while consuming the calendar.
rows.Solution Statement: Eliminate the debt ceiling
rows.Solution Description: Abolish the statutory limit and make debt authority automatic upon enactment of the appropriations and authorizations that create the obligations.
rows.Horizon Justification: Removing the mechanism removes the crisis rather than managing it, and it separates the question of how much to spend from the question of whether to pay for what is already spent.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Raised by five trillion dollars in 2025 inside a reconciliation bill; contested
rows.Concerns: Both parties have used debt ceiling brinkmanship as leverage for unrelated policy demands, and eliminating the mechanism gives up that leverage for whichever party next wants to extract concessions from a must-pass bill.
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: The budget resolution process no longer functions
rows.Problem Description: Thirteen of fifty fiscal years since 1976 had no budget resolution, all since 1999; the April deadline has been met four times since 1986; the process waits on a late presidential submission.
rows.Solution Statement: Redesign the budget resolution process
rows.Solution Description: Combine proposed elements: biennial resolution with annual appropriations; May 1 completion in odd years; annual rather than optional reconciliation; no required start from the President's budget; separate budgets and rules for capital, mandatory, and discretionary spending; appropriations and revenue committee leaders on the budget committees; calendar-year fiscal year.
rows.Horizon Justification: It rebuilds the decision structure rather than the deadline; composition and sequencing decide who is in the room when the numbers are set.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
Elements advanced by the 2018 Joint Select Committee, which deadlocked
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 87: Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need statutory revisions to the Congressional Budget Act.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 87 (tracker Rec 87): Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need statutory revisions to the Congressional Budget Act.
rows.Concerns: Combining biennial budgeting, mandatory reconciliation, and new budget committee seats redistributes power among Budget, Appropriations, and tax writing committees, so each has reason to resist the pieces of the package that shrink its own role.
rows.Sources:
Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 87, 88, 92
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562/pdf/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562.pdf

rows.Problem Statement: Fiscal decisions have no enforceable target
rows.Problem Description: Statutory caps have lapsed, statutory pay-as-you-go has never triggered, and the annual process reaches neither revenue nor the tax expenditures that projections put in the trillions.
rows.Solution Statement: Statutory fiscal targets with enforcement triggers
rows.Solution Description: Adopt a multiyear plan built on targets, triggers, and transparency: annual debt or debt-to-GDP targets enforced through a special reconciliation process, a trigger split between spending reductions and revenue increases reaching the broadest possible base including tax expenditures and mandatory health programs, extended baseline projections out twenty-five to thirty years, and caps with statutory enforcement.
rows.Horizon Justification: Binding targets change what the process must produce rather than when it must produce it, which is the difference between a schedule and a constraint.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
Multiple competing versions in circulation; the underlying proposals contradict each other on scope
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 91: Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need a statutory revision to the Congressional Budget Act.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 91 (tracker Rec 91): Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need a statutory revision to the Congressional Budget Act.
rows.Concerns: Statutory pay-as-you-go already exists and has never triggered because Congress routinely waives it, and a new reconciliation-enforced target faces the same waiver pressure once it reaches the mandatory health programs and tax expenditures any trigger would have to cut.
rows.Sources:
Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 91
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562/pdf/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562.pdf

rows.Problem Statement: Programs are funded indefinitely without review
rows.Problem Description: Obsolete and overlapping programs persist because nothing forces a periodic justification, and expired authorizations continue to receive appropriations by default.
rows.Solution Statement: Zero-based budgeting on a rotating cycle with a sunset commission
rows.Solution Description: Require every program to be justified from zero on a ten-year rotation, with a standing sunset commission recommending eliminations and consolidations and a defined path for its recommendations to receive a vote.
rows.Horizon Justification: It makes review a condition of continued funding rather than an optional exercise, which is the mechanism missing behind unauthorized appropriations.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed; versions exist at the state level
rows.Concerns: The ten-year justification cycle multiplies committee workload every year a fraction of the government is up for zero-based review, and the sunset commission's recommendations still depend on the floor vote that expired authorizations already lack today.
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Delegated war and emergency powers never return to Congress
rows.Problem Description: Authorities delegated for specific circumstances persist for decades, and emergency declarations are used to justify action that Congress never affirmatively approved.
rows.Solution Statement: Periodic reauthorization of war and emergency powers
rows.Solution Description: Revise the war powers and emergency powers statutes to require affirmative congressional ratification of declarations and force authorizations, with fast-tracked up-or-down votes to reauthorize on a regular cycle, so lapsed authority expires by default rather than persisting.
rows.Horizon Justification: It reverses the default: authority returns to Congress unless renewed, which changes the structural direction of delegation rather than contesting individual uses of it.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed in multiple forms
rows.Concerns: The default only flips if Congress reliably holds the scheduled votes; the same political incentives that discourage today's rarely used disapproval resolutions turn periodic reauthorization into a reflexive renewal rather than genuine reconsideration.
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Congress has delegated major questions and waits for courts to settle them
rows.Problem Description: Significant policy is made through agency rulemaking that Congress never votes on, and the resulting disputes are resolved in litigation years later.
rows.Solution Statement: Fast-tracked votes on major regulations
rows.Solution Description: Require periodic fast-tracked up-or-down votes to enact proposed major regulations and major changes to them, so the significant choices agencies make return to Congress on a defined schedule.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes where major policy decisions are made, and it forces Congress to legislate on questions it currently leaves to agencies and courts.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed; related to post-Chevron proposals
rows.Concerns: This resembles the REINS Act, which has passed the House repeatedly since 2011 without becoming law; giving Congress veto power over major rules invites gridlock that leaves significant regulations in limbo rather than resolved.
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Congress cannot independently assess regulations
rows.Problem Description: Agencies produce and analyze their own rules, and Congress has no analytic body of its own to assess proposed or existing regulations, so the record it reviews is the one the regulator wrote.
rows.Solution Statement: Congressional Regulation Office
rows.Solution Description: Create a nonpartisan regulation office serving both chambers to analyze proposed and existing rules, paired with increased GAO and CBO funding, alongside a trends-focused technology assessment function.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates analytic capacity Congress owns on the questions where the executive currently holds the entire record, which is the precondition for regulatory oversight after Chevron.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed by several groups
rows.Concerns: A new office competes for the same constrained Legislative Branch appropriation as GAO and CBO, and Congress defunded the similarly conceived Office of Technology Assessment in 1995 once its analysis became politically inconvenient.
rows.Sources:
Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)
Working Group Reform Options Package (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Inspectors general answer to the agencies they investigate
rows.Problem Description: IGs are nominally independent yet depend on the agencies they audit for appointment or daily accountability, a vulnerability politically motivated removals exploit, and their findings never structurally feed congressional work.
rows.Solution Statement: Realign inspectors general toward Congress
rows.Solution Description: Shift IG reporting from agency heads to the Comptroller General, or make IGs congressional employees, operational independence intact. Removal only for cause, with written notice to Congress and appeal rights; budget requests sent directly to Congress unmodified, with a funding floor; a quarterly IG and GAO council feeding oversight.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes who the executive branch's internal auditors answer to, the root of every removal fight and of findings that never reach Congress.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed in two forms with different destinations
rows.Concerns: Shifting IG appointment or removal to Congress invites a separation-of-powers challenge under unitary executive theory, and agency heads who value IG cooperation on their own terms have no incentive to support a change that ends that leverage.
rows.Sources:
Functional Fusion (April 2026)
Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Leadership overrides appropriators unilaterally
rows.Problem Description: Subcommittee chairs no longer hold the influence the position once carried; leadership can override a committee recommendation without a vote, so the committee's work is provisional until leadership agrees with it.
rows.Solution Statement: Require a House vote to override an appropriations recommendation
rows.Solution Description: Change the rules so overriding an Appropriations Committee recommendation requires a vote of the House rather than a leadership decision.
rows.Horizon Justification: It moves a decision from one office to the chamber, restoring the committee's product as the default rather than an opening offer.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed by staff and outside experts
rows.Concerns: Leadership holds the override power today and controls the rules process that would have to surrender it, so adoption depends on leaders agreeing to give up discretion they currently use freely.
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Members cannot object to unauthorized spending
rows.Problem Description: More than thirteen hundred authorizations had expired before FY2025, with hundreds of billions in appropriations tied to them, and no individual member has a procedural way to force the question.
rows.Solution Statement: Member challenge right against unauthorized appropriations
rows.Solution Description: Give each member one challenge per session against any unfunded mandate or unauthorized appropriation, requiring a House vote to override the objection, with an additional challenge earned if the objection is upheld.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates an individual member power where none exists and attaches a cost to funding lapsed authorizations, which is what makes the authorization step meaningful again.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed by staff and outside experts
rows.Concerns: With over thirteen hundred expired authorizations, one challenge per member per session addresses a small fraction of them, and leadership can still marshal the votes to override a challenge on any program it wants to protect.
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Voters have no clear signal on fiscal accountability
rows.Problem Description: Fiscal arguments run on assertion, and constituents have no straightforward account of what the Congress they are about to vote on did to the deficit.
rows.Solution Statement: Pre-election CBO letter to taxpayers
rows.Solution Description: Require CBO to send taxpayers a plain-language letter before each congressional election stating the deficit and the current Congress's effect on it.
rows.Horizon Justification: It is a disclosure that changes no decision rights and depends entirely on voters acting on information they have largely had access to already.
rows.Path to H2+: No H2+ successor in this database. None of the candidates is a genuine successor; what is needed is an H2+ that embeds fiscal disclosure into a standing, institution-owned accountability mechanism, such as a statutory scorecard tying committee action to deficit outcomes, rather than a one-time pre-election letter.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed
rows.Concerns: CBO becomes a preelection target for whichever party dislikes its numbers, and the letter creates no new decision right, so it changes what voters are told without changing any incentive driving the deficit it describes.
rows.Sources: Rebuild Congress Initiative, Budget and Appropriations Pre-Read (Aug 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Congress and agencies set priorities in parallel and never reconcile them
rows.Problem Description: Agencies produce strategic and performance plans under existing law without any structured congressional engagement, so the branch that writes the mandate never states which priorities it endorses.
rows.Solution Statement: Joint agency performance plan review
rows.Solution Description: Require each agency to submit its annual performance plan to committees of jurisdiction for a structured review of at least sixty days before finalization. Committees issue a formal statement recording priorities endorsed, priorities requested but not adopted, and points of disagreement, and agencies must respond in writing explaining how that input was or was not incorporated.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates a recurring, documented moment where the two branches state priorities to each other, which is the loop that currently does not exist at any point in the cycle.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; not introduced
rows.Concerns: Agencies must respond in writing but nothing obligates them to adopt committee priorities, so the review can become a paper exercise that documents disagreement without resolving it, while adding sixty days to agency planning.
rows.Sources: Functional Fusion (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Diagnosis happens inside the executive branch and arrives filtered
rows.Problem Description: Agencies analyze what is going wrong in a program, political messaging shapes that analysis before it reaches the Hill, and it lands with committee staff who have no structured forum to engage it.
rows.Solution Statement: Cross-branch diagnostic working groups
rows.Solution Description: Give committees standing authority to convene working groups on high-priority issues, jointly staffed by committee staff, career agency staff, and GAO, co-chaired by a member and a senior agency official, with required bipartisan staff participation. Each group publishes interim updates and a final joint report of findings, implementation barriers, and policy options. The chair holds an independent right to release findings, so neither branch can suppress them.
rows.Horizon Justification: It puts congressional and agency staff in a shared analytic process with a protected right of publication, changing where diagnosis is done rather than how it is received.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; not introduced
rows.Concerns: Agency political leadership loses control over what career staff say publicly, since the chair's independent publication right can surface findings the administration would rather manage internally, giving agencies reason to limit who participates.
rows.Sources: Functional Fusion (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Minor statutory fixes wait years for a vehicle
rows.Problem Description: Agencies find technical corrections through implementation: small in substance, large in operation, and never worth floor time on their own.
rows.Solution Statement: Technical corrections fast-track docket
rows.Solution Description: Establish a quarterly docket for agency-submitted statutory clarifications, exceptions, and waivers from implementation. GAO and the Parliamentarian jointly certify each as non-substantive; the subcommittee approves or rejects within a set period; approved items ride one consolidated vehicle with expedited floor procedure and a germaneness bar.
rows.Horizon Justification: It clears technical debt without changing how legislation is developed, and certification holds it to changes that are not policy.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #27. The quarterly technical-corrections docket proves agencies and Congress can process small statutory fixes through a certified pipeline, a workflow a version-controlled US Code with consolidated drafting offices would run continuously rather than reassembling case by case each quarter.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; called the most immediately achievable element of its package
rows.Concerns: The germaneness bar depends on GAO and the Parliamentarian correctly distinguishing technical fixes from substantive policy every quarter, and an error either lets policy ride through unreviewed or strands a genuine fix that looks contestable.
rows.Sources: Functional Fusion (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Congress cannot authorize a test of anything
rows.Problem Description: Waivers and pilot authorities are granted sparingly and inconsistently, so alternatives cannot be tried at small scale with congressional visibility. Policy changes arrive all at once or not at all.
rows.Solution Statement: Subcommittee pilot and demonstration authority
rows.Solution Description: Give each subcommittee an annual authorization to approve a limited number of pilots at agencies in its jurisdiction, each with defined objectives, timeframe, evaluation plan, and supplemental appropriations within set parameters. GAO evaluates each pilot on completion, and the subcommittee makes a public determination to scale, redesign, or discontinue, with written rationale. The authority is structured as a condition on delegated authority rather than a legislative veto.
rows.Horizon Justification: It gives Congress a way to learn from a bounded experiment before legislating at scale, a capability the institution has no mechanism for.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; not introduced
rows.Concerns: Subcommittees control which pilots get approved, so the mechanism risks testing only proposals that do not threaten existing arrangements, and a pilot GAO recommends scaling still needs separate legislation to become permanent.
rows.Sources: Functional Fusion (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Every resource shift requires a full appropriations cycle
rows.Problem Description: Moving money in response to what implementation reveals means waiting for the next bill, so programs run against last year's assumptions until the calendar allows a correction.
rows.Solution Statement: Delegated reprogramming authority for authorizing subcommittees
rows.Solution Description: Grant subcommittees of jurisdiction a defined reprogramming authority within parameters set by the relevant appropriations subcommittee. Agencies submit written justification, subcommittees act within a defined period with approval deemed on inaction, and all approved reprogrammings are publicly reported. Appropriations subcommittees set annual dollar thresholds and eligibility.
rows.Horizon Justification: It distributes a piece of spending discretion to the committees that hold the subject matter knowledge, changing who can act on implementation information and how fast.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; appropriators would contest it
rows.Concerns: Appropriations subcommittees have long guarded reprogramming as their own prerogative, and handing authorizing committees a share of spending discretion is a jurisdictional loss that Appropriations has resisted in past attempts to distribute this authority.
rows.Sources: Functional Fusion (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Every bill is treated the same regardless of the work behind it
rows.Problem Description: A bill developed through evidence and joint diagnosis has no better path than one introduced for a press release, so nothing in the process rewards doing the work.
rows.Solution Statement: Evidence-grounded legislation pathway
rows.Solution Description: Create a defined pathway for bills developed out of joint diagnostic working groups. Qualifying bills carry a GAO-validated implementation assessment documenting findings, options considered, and the evidence base, and receive a guaranteed markup vote within a defined period plus priority floor scheduling. GAO maintains a public registry, and each member has an annual allocation of supported bills.
rows.Horizon Justification: It attaches procedural advantage to evidence rather than to sponsorship or leadership favor, which changes what members are rewarded for doing.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; explicitly creates two tiers of legislation
rows.Concerns: Guaranteed markup and floor priority create an incentive to manufacture a qualifying diagnostic process rather than pursue one honestly, and offices with more staff capacity to produce GAO-validated documentation gain an advantage unrelated to a bill's merits.
rows.Sources: Functional Fusion (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: GAO serves two branches and arrives after the fact
rows.Problem Description: GAO operates as a retrospective auditor at the end of the process, houses functions that belong to the executive branch, and engages with legislation only once problems are embedded in law.
rows.Solution Statement: Realign and expand GAO as an institution of Congress
rows.Solution Description: Amend GAO's organic statute to establish it as an institution of Congress serving the legislative branch exclusively, transferring executive functions to the relevant agencies. Expand its mission to cover cross-branch facilitation, early-stage policy analysis, and statutory interpretation support, with organizationally distinct units and a structural firewall between audit and advisory work, producing implementation assessments of major legislation under consideration at committee request.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes what GAO is for and when it engages, converting the branch's largest analytic asset from an after-action reviewer into a design capability.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; not introduced
rows.Concerns: Combining early design advice with audit work risks GAO's standing as an independent after-the-fact reviewer, since a committee GAO advised while drafting a bill has reason to expect a friendlier evaluation later, whatever firewall separates the two units on paper.
rows.Sources: Functional Fusion (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Almost all congressional staff are partisan appointees
rows.Problem Description: Nearly all of roughly thirty thousand staff serve at a member's pleasure, fitting for representation but leaving policy analysis, drafting, and implementation assessment without continuity across elections or a shared factual base.
rows.Solution Statement: Nonpartisan congressional staff corps
rows.Solution Description: Create within GAO a corps of roughly three thousand career civil servants, reclassified from existing positions, supporting committees in policy analysis, drafting, working group staffing, and implementation assessment. They hold civil service protections; the Comptroller General appoints them in consultation with committee leadership; partisan activity is barred on duty.
rows.Horizon Justification: A permanent professional layer survives elections, something every comparable institution has and Congress lacks.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; the largest staffing proposal in this set
rows.Concerns: Members lose direct control over three thousand analytic positions that currently answer only to them, and a career corps housed in GAO can produce analysis members disregard when it conflicts with the political case they want to make.
rows.Sources: Functional Fusion (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Agency knowledge reaches the Hill only through filtered channels
rows.Problem Description: Committees learn what agencies know through testimony, written responses, and technical assistance requests, all delayed and shaped politically, so the operational detail that would inform legislating never arrives in usable form.
rows.Solution Statement: Agency liaison offices inside the Capitol complex
rows.Solution Description: Require each agency above a defined budget threshold to maintain a physical liaison office in the Capitol complex, staffed by career civil servants with operational program expertise and subject to a minimum tenure requirement, supplying timely operational information to staff on request and supporting committee engagement across the cycle.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates a permanent, career-staffed channel between the branches that does not run through political appointees, changing what information is available and how quickly.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; not introduced
rows.Concerns: Every qualifying agency funding a physical Capitol office is a recurring cost across many agencies, and liaisons still answer to agency leadership, so the channel can end up filtered by the same incentives it was built to bypass.
rows.Sources: Functional Fusion (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Drafting does not account for how a statute will be implemented or read
rows.Problem Description: After Loper Bright, imprecise statutory language produces litigation and instability rather than executive latitude, and Congress has no in-house expertise on how to structure delegated authority that survives constitutional constraints.
rows.Solution Statement: Modernize Legislative Counsel for post-Chevron drafting
rows.Solution Description: Direct House and Senate Legislative Counsel, coordinating with GAO, to expand drafting assistance to reflect operational feasibility and to build expertise in administrative law and program implementation. They would advise members on lawfully structuring conditions on delegated authority, pilot authorizations, and reprogramming, produce interpretation guidance on committee request, and report annually on interpretive questions that warrant legislation.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes what drafting expertise covers at the moment statutes are written, which determines how much interpretive room courts and agencies have later.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; not introduced
rows.Concerns: Legislative Counsel's value rests on confidential, nonpartisan drafting assistance, and asking it to also publish annual interpretive guidance pulls it toward substantive policy judgments that compromise the neutrality members currently rely on.
rows.Sources: Functional Fusion (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: The executive workforce answers to the President rather than to statute
rows.Problem Description: Political appointees have grown from roughly a thousand in the early 1960s to about four thousand today, thickening a layer that makes agencies more responsive to presidential direction than to faithful execution of legislative mandates.
rows.Solution Statement: Reduce the number of political appointees
rows.Solution Description: Direct a review of all political appointee positions within a year of enactment, identifying those convertible to career status, and set a government-wide reduction target returning toward pre-Watergate levels, to be achieved over four years.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes who executes the laws Congress writes, which conditions whether any oversight or implementation reform reaches the people doing the work.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Drafted as illustrative bill text; contested across administrations
rows.Concerns: Every administration since Watergate has resisted ceding appointment power, and a four-year phase-in run by the same executive branch being reduced gives future administrations wide discretion over which positions actually convert to career status.
rows.Sources: Functional Fusion (April 2026)

rows.Problem Statement: Congressional productivity is measured by counting bills
rows.Problem Description: Bill counts ignore the tendency to bundle many items into single large measures and treat a landmark statute and a post office naming as equivalent, so the institution is assessed on a number that describes almost nothing.
rows.Solution Statement: Measure output by significant policy change rather than bill count
rows.Solution Description: Adopt a measure of productivity based on laws that alter existing government policy to a significant degree, applied consistently over time, in place of counts of public laws enacted.
rows.Horizon Justification: A better metric changes how the institution is described without changing anything it does, and metrics become distorting as soon as anyone optimizes for them.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #140. Adopting a measure that separates substantive policy change from bill-count padding supplies the definition and evidentiary standard an evidence-grounded pathway needs to certify which bills qualify for guaranteed markup and priority floor scheduling.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Long-standing academic proposal
rows.Concerns: Defining what counts as a significant policy change is itself a judgment call subject to dispute, and adopting a better metric changes how the institution is described without touching any incentive that drives what members introduce.
rows.Sources: Vox, Congressional Dysfunction (Ezra Klein, citing David Mayhew)

rows.Problem Statement: Large technology projects are funded on schedule rather than results
rows.Problem Description: Large House technology projects are funded through multiyear waterfall models, with no way to adjust or discontinue a project based on what it has produced.
rows.Solution Statement: Milestone-based technology funding
rows.Solution Description: Disburse the Modernization Initiatives Fund in tranches released against demonstrated working functionality rather than elapsed schedule, with a user-testing gate before each subsequent tranche. Give the fund explicit discontinuation authority that treats early termination of a failing project as a successful process outcome, cap the initial tranche to force decomposition, and report to House Administration on adjusted and discontinued projects alongside completed ones.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes how money is released and who can stop a project, which determines whether failure is caught early. Low cost and implementable as internal policy.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed; not adopted
rows.Concerns: Success depends on House Administration actually enforcing discontinuation against a project's sponsors and vendor, who have every incentive to soften a testing gate rather than accept an early kill, and internal policy can be relaxed with no floor vote required.
rows.Sources: Recoding America ModSub Submissions (2026)

rows.Additional Tags: CAO, Organization, Operations, Coordination, Data, Transparency
rows.Problem Statement: No one knows which CAO unit owns which service
rows.Problem Description: Offices, vendors, and outside stakeholders cannot tell which unit to approach for which service, so requests route through personal networks.
rows.Solution Statement: Publish a CAO organizational chart
rows.Solution Description: Publish a chart covering each unit, its functional responsibilities, and a designated point of contact. Maintain an internal version with full contact detail and a public version using role-based contacts to limit solicitation and social engineering exposure. Update at minimum at the start of each Congress and after any reorganization, with a named owner.
rows.Horizon Justification: It documents an existing structure rather than changing who decides, and its value decays as soon as the update cadence slips.
rows.Path to H2+: H2+ #19. Publishing which CAO unit owns which service gives requesters the routing information a shared ticketing system needs to direct each request to the correct owner automatically, turning a static chart into a live, trackable request pipeline.
rows.Current Status (Optional): Proposed; not adopted
rows.Concerns: Nothing enforces the update requirement beyond a named owner, so the chart goes stale the same way informal knowledge does now, and requests keep routing through personal networks until people trust it is current.
rows.Sources: Recoding America ModSub Submissions (2026)

rows.Additional Tags: Professional Development, Leadership, In-House Development, Norms
rows.Problem Statement: New supervisors get management authority with no training
rows.Problem Description: Congressional offices promote staff into supervisory roles based on legislative expertise, not management skill, and no institution-wide curriculum teaches cultural competency or how to run an inclusive team. Supervisors improvise, and the quality of management a staffer experiences depends on who happens to run their office.
rows.Solution Statement: Require formal management training for supervisors
rows.Solution Description: Fund and deliver formal management training for staff who supervise others, covering core management skills, cultural competency, and how to sustain an inclusive workplace. Training runs through an in house channel like the Congressional Staff Academy so every new supervisor completes it before or shortly after taking on the role.
rows.Horizon Justification: It adds a training requirement layered onto the existing structure without creating a permanent office that owns supervisor development, so the fix depends on continued funding and enforcement rather than being self-sustaining.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 98: Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: CAO Coaches began providing new classroom and virtual training courses in management and leadership, among other topics.
rows.Concerns: A training requirement easily becomes a compliance box to check, since no office owns ongoing accountability for whether supervisors apply what they learned, and funding for the curriculum can lapse with a shift in appropriations priorities.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 98
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646/pdf/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646.pdf
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: No standing body reviews and updates House staff benefits
rows.Problem Description: House staff benefits are set piecemeal, changed when a single issue draws attention rather than on any regular cycle. No office is tasked with tracking how benefits compare to the outside labor market or recommending updates, so gaps persist until they show up in retention numbers.
rows.Solution Statement: Establish a standing Task Force on the House Workforce
rows.Solution Description: Create a permanent task force, led by the Chief Administrative Officer and drawing members from other House offices, charged with reviewing staff benefits on an ongoing basis and issuing policy recommendations, informed by regular staff surveys on pay, benefits, and quality of life. The task force gives the House a standing mechanism to keep benefits current instead of waiting for a crisis to prompt a fix.
rows.Horizon Justification: A standing task force under the CAO is a permanent institutional body with an ongoing mandate, so benefit reviews continue independent of any single champion or one-time push.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 99: Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: The Task Force on the House Workforce was named in the report accompanying the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 15 (tracker Rec 10): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The Office of Diversity and Inclusion carried out staff surveys in 2019 and 2021. The CAO's new Office of Talent and Development now conducts such surveys.
rows.Concerns: The task force can issue recommendations but holds no authority to compel offices or House Administration to fund them, so persistent gaps survive the survey findings the same way they survive today's ad hoc attention.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 99
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646/pdf/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646.pdf
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 15
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562/pdf/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562.pdf

rows.Problem Statement: Staff must pay out of pocket for certification programs
rows.Problem Description: Certification programs exist for many staff roles, from IT to procurement to communications, but offices have no clear authority to pay for them. Staff who want a credential either cover the cost themselves or go without, and the answer varies office by office.
rows.Solution Statement: Authorize office-funded certifications and expand Academy-delivered ones
rows.Solution Description: Allow member, committee, and leadership offices to pay for professional development opportunities that lead to a certification, using existing office budgets, and expand certifications offered directly through the nonpartisan Congressional Staff Academy's own curriculum. Staff gain two paths to a credential in their field: an office-funded outside program or an Academy-delivered certification alongside its existing trainings.
rows.Horizon Justification: Authorizing office spending and expanding Academy certifications each help some staff reach a credential, but neither guarantees coverage: office funding still depends on each office's budget, and Academy offerings depend on what the Academy chooses to include in its curriculum, so an institution-wide standard remains absent.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 102: Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: CHA updated the Members' Congressional Handbook to allow for office reimbursement of job-related professional development programs that provide a certification.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 16 (tracker Rec 63): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: CAO offers career-path course work through the Congressional Staff Academy, as well as certifications for specific skills and classes. Full implementation would include role-specific certifications.
rows.Concerns: Larger or better-funded offices will pay for certifications while leaner offices will not, widening the same office-by-office disparity in staff development the reform is meant to fix, since nothing sets a common floor.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 102
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646/pdf/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646.pdf
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 16
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562/pdf/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562.pdf

rows.Problem Statement: Contract employees lack access to House employee assistance services
rows.Problem Description: Contractors who work on the Capitol campus alongside House staff are not covered by the Office of Employee Assistance, even though they work the same halls under the same pressures. Coverage depends entirely on what their employer, not the House, chooses to offer.
rows.Solution Statement: Extend employee assistance services to contract staff
rows.Solution Description: Direct the House to work with its contractors, where feasible, so Capitol campus contract employees have access to assistance services comparable to what the Office of Employee Assistance provides House staff. Coverage is negotiated contract by contract rather than guaranteed outright.
rows.Horizon Justification: Coverage runs through individual contract negotiations rather than a House-owned guarantee, so it depends on what each contractor agrees to and can lapse when a contract changes.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 104: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: CAO and CHA have reviewed and validated that these services are in place for larger contractors working in the Capitol complex.
rows.Concerns: Coverage depends on what each contractor agrees to fund, so a firm can decline or drop it at the next recompete, and turnover in Capitol campus contracts means the benefit can vanish with no notice to the workers who relied on it.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 104
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646/pdf/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646.pdf
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: Office of Employee Assistance lacks bilingual and trauma care capacity
rows.Problem Description: The Office of Employee Assistance is the main mental health and crisis resource for House staff, but it does not consistently offer bilingual services or clinicians trained in trauma care. Staff whose first language is not English, or who need trauma-specific support, may not find it inside the office meant to serve them.
rows.Solution Statement: Build bilingual and trauma capacity into Employee Assistance
rows.Solution Description: Direct the Office of Employee Assistance to recruit and retain a diverse staff, offer services in languages beyond English, and keep clinicians on staff who are trained to provide trauma care. The office becomes able to serve a wider range of staff needs without referring them elsewhere.
rows.Horizon Justification: It builds durable clinical capacity inside an office the House already owns and staffs permanently, so the improvement holds without depending on outside grants or a one-time hire.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 105: Closed-Resolved. 117th Congress: Report language encouraging this was included in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022; need additional information from the Office of Employee Assistance.
rows.Concerns: Recruiting bilingual clinicians trained in trauma care means competing against private practices that pay more, and the office has to fund permanent positions rather than one time grants, so the improvement rests on a sustained hiring budget appropriators do not guarantee.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 105
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646/pdf/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646.pdf
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: The Student Loan Repayment Program excludes tuition assistance
rows.Problem Description: The House offers a Student Loan Repayment Program for staff who already carry education debt, but nothing helps staff currently pursuing further education pay tuition. Staff who want to finish a degree or add a credential cover tuition themselves.
rows.Solution Statement: Expand loan repayment into tuition assistance
rows.Solution Description: Broaden the Student Loan Repayment Program so it also covers tuition assistance, letting the House support staff who are paying for education now rather than only those repaying debt from the past. The same program administers both benefits.
rows.Horizon Justification: It widens an existing benefit rather than changing who owns staff education support, so the fix is a funding expansion layered onto a program that already exists.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 106: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: Language was passed into law with the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, P.L. 117-328. 119th Congress: CHA promulgated new regulations and renamed the program.
rows.Concerns: The Student Loan Repayment Program already competes for a limited personnel budget line, so adding tuition assistance without new money forces offices to choose between past debt and current tuition, and Congress still has to appropriate the increase.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 106
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646/pdf/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646.pdf
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: Offices manage recruitment and hiring without dedicated software
rows.Problem Description: House offices post jobs, screen resumes, and track candidates using whatever spreadsheet or email chain a chief of staff sets up, since no shared recruitment tool exists. Turnover means every new office rebuilds the same manual process.
rows.Solution Statement: Provide House offices talent acquisition software
rows.Solution Description: Have the Chief Administrative Officer provide access to industry-leading talent acquisition software so offices can manage job postings, applications, and candidate tracking through one system instead of building their own. Adoption is voluntary and offices keep their own hiring decisions.
rows.Horizon Justification: It supplies a shared tool but leaves each office's hiring practice untouched and adoption optional, so an office that skips it is back to the same manual process.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 107: Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: CAO is making new software available for offices and began enrolling participants at New Member Orientation.
rows.Concerns: Adoption is voluntary, so an office whose chief of staff already runs hiring off email and spreadsheets has no reason to switch, and the tool leaves each office's hiring practice and turnover problem exactly as it was.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 107
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646/pdf/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646.pdf
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: Offices set intern stipends without cost of living information
rows.Problem Description: Offices decide what to pay interns with no shared reference for what it actually costs an intern to live near the Capitol. Stipends vary widely, and a low stipend can quietly exclude interns who cannot cover rent and food in Washington on their own.
rows.Solution Statement: Publish intern cost of living information for offices
rows.Solution Description: Have the Chief Administrative Officer compile and provide House offices with information on the cost of living for interns, so offices can set stipends against an actual benchmark rather than a guess. The information itself does not set a floor; offices decide what to do with it.
rows.Horizon Justification: It supplies a reference number rather than a stipend requirement, so an office can still set a stipend that leaves an intern unable to afford living in Washington.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 109: Closed-Resolved. 119th Congress: In 2022 the House authorized the House Paid Intern Program, which provides participating offices with a stipend they can use to pay their interns.
rows.Concerns: Publishing a cost of living benchmark does not require any office to pay it, so an office can see the number and still set a stipend that leaves an intern unable to afford Washington rent, which is the problem the reform is meant to fix.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 109
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646/pdf/GPO-CRPT-117hrpt646.pdf
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: House interns and coordinators lack a central support office
rows.Problem Description: The House has no counterpart to a Senate-side intern office; onboarding, curriculum, professional development, and coordinator training are each built office by office. The Senate has moved toward a resource office of its own, leaving the House to run a larger internship program with no institutional home to standardize it.
rows.Solution Statement: Establish a House Intern and Fellowship Program Office
rows.Solution Description: Create an Intern and Fellowship Program Office or coordinator role that owns onboarding, develops shared educational curriculum, runs professional development for interns, and trains the coordinators who manage them across House offices. Offices keep hiring their own interns; the office gives them a common standard to hire and train against.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates a permanent institutional office that owns intern and fellow development House-wide, so the standard persists independent of any one office's initiative.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 110: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: Language to establish the office was passed into law with the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, P.L. 117-328. There is now an Intern and Fellow page on the HR Hub.
rows.Concerns: Standing up a new office means new staff and space inside the House's own budget, and because offices keep hiring their own interns, the office can set a standard without any way to make individual offices follow it.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 110

rows.Problem Statement: Fellows and detailees receive fewer resources than staff
rows.Problem Description: Fellows and detailees often work full legislative or policy roles inside an office, but current rules do not clearly entitle them to the same resources as professional staff, from equipment to system access. Offices are left to interpret or work around the ambiguity individually.
rows.Solution Statement: Clarify rules granting fellows equipment parity
rows.Solution Description: Amend House and Senate rules to state plainly that fellows and detailees receive the same resources and equipment as professional staff. Offices no longer have to interpret ambiguous rules or make case by case exceptions to equip a fellow to do the job they were placed to do.
rows.Horizon Justification: Once the rule is clarified, resource access holds automatically for every future fellow or detailee without further action, which is what makes it self-sustaining.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 111: Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: Implementing language included in H.Res. 1331; need to review existing rules and amend the Members' Congressional Handbook to clarify access by fellows.
rows.Concerns: Changing House and Senate rules requires chamber action in both bodies, and guaranteeing fellows the same equipment as staff means offices absorb an added cost without a matching increase in their operating budget.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 111

rows.Problem Statement: Whether remote internships can continue permanently is unresolved
rows.Problem Description: The House allowed remote internships during the pandemic on a temporary basis, and offices that used it to reach candidates outside Washington do not know whether the option will remain available. Without a permanent policy, offices default back to requiring interns to relocate.
rows.Solution Statement: Study making remote internships permanent
rows.Solution Description: Direct a feasibility study of permanently allowing remote internships, examining what changed under the temporary allowance and what a permanent policy would require. The study does not itself change the internship rules; it produces the basis for a later decision.
rows.Horizon Justification: A feasibility study produces a recommendation, not a rule, so remote internships remain temporary and reversible until a separate decision makes the policy permanent.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 112: Closed-Not Implemented. 119th Congress: The intent was to expand opportunities for individuals who cannot travel to and live in Washington, D.C. Closed without implementation.
rows.Concerns: The study produces a recommendation, not a policy change, and remote internships remain revocable at any point until a separate decision makes the temporary allowance permanent, which studies like it do not guarantee will happen.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 112

rows.Problem Statement: Committees fund intern stipends out of their own budget
rows.Problem Description: Committees that want to pay interns have to draw stipends from the same budget that covers staff salaries and operations, which pushes some committees to leave intern positions unpaid or unfilled. Unpaid internships narrow who can afford to work on a committee.
rows.Solution Statement: Create a separate committee intern stipend allowance
rows.Solution Description: Provide committees a program allowance, separate from their regular operating budget, dedicated to paying interns. Committees can staff internships without trading off against salary or operating lines, and paid positions become the default rather than the exception.
rows.Horizon Justification: The allowance is a budget line that can be adjusted or dropped in a future appropriations cycle, and committees remain free to under-request it, so paid internships are not guaranteed.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 113: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: CHA passed Committee Resolution 118-33 to approve allocation for paid committee internships.
rows.Concerns: The allowance is a discrete appropriations line that can be trimmed or eliminated in a future cycle, and because committees are not required to draw on it, a committee that declines to request funding leaves its unpaid internships in place.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 113

rows.Problem Statement: The Capitol has no accessible drop off point for visitors with mobility impairments
rows.Problem Description: Visitors and staff with mobility impairments must approach the Capitol complex from whatever entrance their vehicle can reach, since no dedicated drop off and pick up zone exists near an accessible entrance and no published process explains how to find one. The gap has no single owner, since it touches AOC facilities, Capitol Police, and House Administration at once.
rows.Solution Statement: Designate an ADA drop off and pick up zone
rows.Solution Description: Designate a drop off and pick up zone near an accessible Capitol entrance and publish a clear process for using it, so visitors and staff with mobility impairments know where to go before they arrive. AOC and Capitol Police coordinate the physical space and the security process around it.
rows.Horizon Justification: It fixes one access point rather than establishing a standing accessibility function that reviews and maintains Capitol infrastructure over time.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 114: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The Modernization Subcommittee sent a letter to the AOC, SAA, and USCP requesting a preliminary study and a temporary solution for Spring 2024.
rows.Concerns: AOC, Capitol Police, and House Administration all touch this and none owns it, so the same coordination gap that stalled a fix for years can just as easily hold up this one, and one entrance does not address the rest of the campus.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 114

rows.Problem Statement: Visitors and staff with disabilities arrive at security screening with no idea what to expect
rows.Problem Description: Capitol security screening involves procedures, equipment, and physical layouts that can be disorienting or inaccessible for people with disabilities, and neither Capitol Police nor the House currently publishes information describing what visitors and staff will encounter. People learn the process by going through it once, which discourages some from visiting or working on the Hill at all.
rows.Solution Statement: Publish security screening information for people with disabilities
rows.Solution Description: Publish clear information describing the security screening techniques and equipment that visitors and staff with disabilities will encounter entering the Capitol complex, distributed through the same channels used for other visitor guidance. Capitol Police and the House compile and keep the material current.
rows.Horizon Justification: It adds published guidance without changing who owns or reviews Capitol security operations for accessibility.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 115: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The U.S. Capitol Police website now provides screening information. The Subcommittee has requested this also be posted with the Capitol Visitor Center.
rows.Concerns: Publishing what to expect does not change the equipment or procedures themselves, so a visitor still faces screening gear and layouts that are disorienting or inaccessible, only now with advance warning instead of a fix.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 115

rows.Problem Statement: Many Capitol doorways require grip strength staff and visitors do not have
rows.Problem Description: Automatic doors are installed unevenly across the Capitol complex, and much of the remaining door hardware requires a firm one handed grasp to operate. Staff and visitors with limited hand strength or mobility face doors they cannot open unassisted at buildings they use every day.
rows.Solution Statement: Install automatic doors and accessible door hardware
rows.Solution Description: Prioritize installing additional automatic doors and replacing door hardware that is difficult to grasp with one hand across House buildings. AOC carries out the installation as part of its ongoing facilities work.
rows.Horizon Justification: It replaces hardware building by building rather than setting a standing accessibility standard that governs future construction and renovation.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 116: Open-Needs Attention. 118th Congress: Making all doors accessible requires significant investment in funding and staff. The AOC has made cost estimates available but adequate funding has not been appropriated.
rows.Concerns: Retrofitting doors and hardware across House buildings is a facilities budget item competing with other AOC priorities, and doing it building by building without a standard for new construction means future renovations can reintroduce the same hardware.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 116

rows.Problem Statement: Member and committee websites are not reliably built or kept accessible
rows.Problem Description: Federal accessibility requirements apply to member and committee websites, but awareness of those requirements varies by office, and staff often lack training or tools to keep a site compliant as it is updated. Constituents who use assistive technology cannot reliably use the site of the office that represents them.
rows.Solution Statement: Train and tool House offices to maintain accessible websites
rows.Solution Description: Promote awareness of website accessibility requirements across member and committee offices and give staff standing training and tools to maintain and update accessible sites, rather than leaving offices to discover requirements only after a complaint. The House sustains the training and tooling as staff and site features turn over.
rows.Horizon Justification: It establishes a standing, institution run training and tooling function rather than a one time compliance check, so accessibility holds as staff and sites change.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 117: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: House Web Services hosted an event on July 24, 2023 on web accessibility and Section 508 compliance, and reviewed member site ratings.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 33 (tracker Rec 27): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: Pursuant to H. Res. 756, CAO is nearing completion on bringing all CAO-controlled websites into compliance.
rows.Concerns: Training and tools are made available to offices, but nothing here compels an office to keep its site accessible, so a site can still drift out of compliance when staff turn over or a redesign skips the training entirely.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 117

rows.Problem Statement: New Member Orientation doubles as a party leadership event
rows.Problem Description: New Member Orientation is currently intertwined with party leadership events, so incoming members' first structured experience of Congress emphasizes party organization over the civility, collaboration, and leadership skills they will need to legislate. Moving orientation to a bipartisan body, on its own, does not specify what orientation should teach.
rows.Solution Statement: Add a civility and collaboration curriculum, held apart from leadership events
rows.Solution Description: Hold New Member Orientation separately from party leadership events and build its curriculum around civility, collaboration, and leadership skills rather than party organization. The bipartisan body running orientation designs and delivers this content each term.
rows.Horizon Justification: It changes what orientation teaches and where it sits on the calendar, but leaves orientation as a single term opening event rather than a standing, term long program.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 118: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: Programming was included during the most recent NMO for members elected to the 119th Congress highlighting the importance of civility and collaboration.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 30 (tracker Rec 14): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The 117th and 118th Congress NMO programs included sessions where decorum and bipartisanship were discussed.
rows.Concerns: Separating orientation from leadership events changes one week at the start of a term rather than the leadership dynamics that shape a member's first months, and party leadership loses an early captive audience it currently uses to organize incoming members before anyone else does.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 118
