rows.Problem Statement: Bill referral to committee is tracked manually and inconsistently
rows.Problem Description: When a bill is introduced, referral to committee and any subsequent progress through the legislative process is recorded through manual, largely paper based procedures. There is no automated system that tracks a bill's status as it moves, so staff and the public rely on periodic updates rather than a live record.
rows.Solution Statement: Automate bill referral and progress tracking
rows.Solution Description: The House builds a system that automates bill referral to committee and tracks the bill's status as it moves through the legislative process. Staff and the public see where a bill stands without waiting on a manual update, and referral decisions are recorded in a structured, queryable form.
rows.Horizon Justification: Once built, an automated referral and tracking system becomes the institution's standing record of how bills move, replacing manual tracking rather than adding a tool on top of it.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 167: Open-In Progress. 119th Congress: Construction of the Committee Activity Portal has developed its initial three modules: Committee Vote, Committee Referral, and Committee Membership.
rows.Concerns: Building an authoritative referral and status system is a substantial technology undertaking, and it turns a process the Parliamentarian's office currently handles case by case into a structured record that constrains that discretion.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 167

rows.Problem Statement: Loan repayment assistance counts against the pay cap for expert staff
rows.Problem Description: House staff compensation is capped, and student loan repayment assistance currently counts toward that cap. Offices trying to hire or retain staff with specialized expertise, who often carry meaningful student debt, have less room under the cap to offer competitive pay once loan assistance is included.
rows.Solution Statement: Exempt student loan repayment from the pay cap and strengthen the program
rows.Solution Description: The House exempts student loan repayment assistance from the maximum compensation calculation, so offices can offer it without eating into the salary room available under the cap, and increases the financial stability of the Student Loan Repayment Program itself for participating staff. Offices gain an additional tool for retaining expert staff without a separate appropriation.
rows.Horizon Justification: The pay cap exemption and the program strengthening are both changes to standing House rules and regulations, so they hold without further action once in place.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 168: Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: CHA issued updated regulations for the House Student Loan Repayment Program in June 2022 eliminating the limitation on staff receiving benefits.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 22 (tracker Rec 69): Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: The Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2021 extended this provision through 2025.
rows.Concerns: Exempting loan repayment from the pay cap effectively raises what offices can pay senior staff without new appropriated funds, and leadership has reason to worry it becomes the first of many carve-outs sought against the cap.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 168

rows.Problem Statement: Collecting bill cosponsors runs on paper dear colleague letters
rows.Problem Description: A member seeking cosponsors for a bill typically circulates a paper or PDF dear colleague letter and collects signatures by hand or through informal office to office outreach. Registering a cosponsor with the Clerk still depends on this manual chain, which is slow and produces no structured record until the paperwork is filed.
rows.Solution Statement: Automate cosponsor collection and registration
rows.Solution Description: The House develops a technology solution that lets members solicit, register, and remove their name as cosponsors digitally, replacing the paper dear colleague and signature process. A bill's cosponsor count updates in a structured system as offices sign on or withdraw, instead of waiting on paperwork to be filed with the Clerk.
rows.Horizon Justification: A digital cosponsor system becomes the standing way cosponsorship is recorded, replacing the manual process rather than running alongside it.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 169: Open-In Progress. 117th Congress: The e-Hopper has made it easier to electronically register cosponsors; need to expand this to make it easier to solicit cosponsors.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 48 (tracker Rec 34): Open-In Progress. 117th Congress: Adding cosponsorship electronically was made permanent through the e-Hopper; need House Rules amendments and e-Hopper functionality to permit removal.
rows.Concerns: Digitizing cosponsorship removes the office-to-office outreach that a paper dear colleague letter also serves as a relationship-building exercise, and the system has to become the Clerk's authoritative record, not just a convenience layer, to actually replace paper.
rows.Sources:

rows.Problem Statement: Legislative drafting between offices and HOLC happens over email
rows.Problem Description: Member, committee, and leadership offices draft legislation in coordination with the House Office of Legislative Counsel largely through email attachments and separate document versions. Tracking which draft is current, reconciling edits from multiple offices, and keeping HOLC in the loop all depend on manual back and forth rather than a shared workspace.
rows.Solution Statement: Collaborative drafting tools across offices and HOLC
rows.Solution Description: The House leverages existing enterprise applications and develops additional tools so that member, committee, and leadership offices can draft legislation together with HOLC in a shared, trackable format. Offices see a current draft and its edit history instead of reconciling emailed versions by hand.
rows.Horizon Justification: The recommendation directs the House to explore existing applications and build unspecified additional tools rather than establish a defined standing platform, so it functions as a step toward better drafting infrastructure rather than the infrastructure itself.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 170: Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: House Office of Legislative Counsel has made an initial request to use Modernization Initiatives Account funds to assess a collaborative drafting tool.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 1 (tracker Rec 1): Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: The U.S. Legislative Markup XML schema is now used for U.S. Code provisions, enrolled bills, and public laws. Work to expand this to include committee reports, hearing records, and other legislative documents is in progress with the Clerk's Office.
rows.Concerns: The recommendation directs the House to explore existing tools and build unspecified additions rather than name a platform, so it can stall at the exploration stage, and HOLC's confidentiality obligations make it cautious about a shared workspace open to multiple offices.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 170

rows.Additional Tags: Coordination, Data, Transparency, Operations, Information Silos
rows.Problem Statement: Offices do not know what outside constituent engagement tools exist
rows.Problem Description: Offices that want to improve outreach or adopt new constituent communication tools generally learn about outside organizations and resources through informal networks, vendor outreach, or trial and error. No House-provided resource lays out what is available, so offices with less capacity to research on their own fall behind on tools that better connected offices already use.
rows.Solution Statement: Compile constituent engagement resources and best practices for offices
rows.Solution Description: The House provides offices with information on outside organizations and resources available to support constituent outreach and engagement, including new communication tools, and develops a nonpartisan best practices page on HouseNet covering constituent engagement and service methods. Offices can review what exists and how to do it well in one place rather than relying on whichever vendor or network happens to reach them.
rows.Horizon Justification: The resource and best practices page inform offices of what is available and how to do it well, but adoption stays entirely voluntary and the pages do not change how constituent engagement tools are funded or supported institutionally.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 173: Open-In Progress. 117th Congress: Committee staff have discussed this with CHA; any lists of outside organizations made available to House offices must accord with Committee rules.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 45 (tracker Rec 26): Closed-Implemented. 119th Congress: The Congressional Staff Academy and CAO Coach continue to expand their offerings; CAO has developed resources for caseworkers on a dedicated HouseNet page focused on serving constituents.
rows.Concerns: A resource page tells offices what exists but gives them no added staff time to act on it, so offices already too stretched to research vendors on their own stay too stretched to follow through once the page exists.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 173

rows.Problem Statement: No public platform exists for feedback on pending legislation
rows.Problem Description: Constituents who want to comment on a specific bill while it is pending have no dedicated House platform for doing so. Feedback instead arrives through phone calls, email, and social media, none of which is structured for a member or committee to weigh against other input on the same bill.
rows.Solution Statement: Study a public feedback platform for pending legislation
rows.Solution Description: The House studies and presents options for a public-facing, interactive platform where constituents can offer opinions and feedback on legislation as it moves through the process. The study lays out what such a platform would require before the House commits to building one.
rows.Horizon Justification: A study produces options rather than a platform, so it leaves the underlying gap in structured public input unchanged until a specific design is chosen and funded.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 174: Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need development of a new public-facing constituent engagement interactive platform providing methods beyond email and webforms.
rows.Concerns: The study produces options, not a platform, so the underlying gap in structured public input stays open until a design is funded and built, and any future platform risks being flooded by organized campaigns rather than genuine constituent views.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 174

rows.Problem Statement: Offices lack modern tools for handling constituent correspondence
rows.Problem Description: Offices manage constituent correspondence largely on legacy constituent management systems and manual processes, which slows turnaround time and limits offices' ability to evaluate newer commercial tools before adopting them. The House Digital Service has not systematically reviewed and onboarded correspondence-specific technology on offices' behalf, so each office is left to vet vendors independently.
rows.Solution Statement: HDS evaluation and onboarding of correspondence tools
rows.Solution Description: The House Digital Service evaluates industry leading correspondence technology tools and platforms and onboards the ones that clear review, so offices can respond to constituents faster and improve the quality and substance of correspondence. Offices draw on HDS's vetting instead of researching and negotiating with vendors on their own.
rows.Horizon Justification: HDS vetting speeds up which tools an office can adopt but leaves the office by office procurement and approval pipeline itself unchanged, so the underlying bottleneck in acquiring new technology persists.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 175: Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: The Subcommittee prioritized this through vendor roundtable discussions with the CAO, which is exploring enterprise-wide systems.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 57 (tracker Rec 43): Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: The Communications Standards Commission took several steps to improve dissemination of digital advertisements and disclosure of mass unsolicited emails.
rows.Concerns: HDS vetting speeds up which tools clear review but leaves each office's own procurement and approval steps in place, so the pace of actually adopting a new tool is still set by that unchanged pipeline.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 175

rows.Problem Statement: Committees have no platform to solicit public comment before action
rows.Problem Description: A committee that wants to gather public comment or evidence on a topic before it comes up for action has no dedicated platform for doing so. Committees rely on hearings and ad hoc outreach, which reach a narrower set of voices and happen only after a topic is already on the agenda.
rows.Solution Statement: Study a public comment platform for committees
rows.Solution Description: The House studies and presents options for a platform that lets committees solicit public comment and evidence on topics that may come before them, ahead of formal committee action. The study identifies what such a platform would need before the House builds or funds one.
rows.Horizon Justification: A study produces options rather than a working platform, so committees still lack a channel for pre-hearing public input until a design is chosen and built.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 176: Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need to study the feasibility and level of committee buy-in for a central website or plug-in to solicit public comments.
rows.Concerns: Like the parallel proposal for legislation, this produces options rather than a working platform, and any comment channel built on top of it risks being dominated by organized campaigns rather than the broader public it is meant to reach.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 176

rows.Problem Statement: Constituent tour requests are tracked ad hoc across offices
rows.Problem Description: Every House office fields Capitol tour requests from constituents, but there is no shared system for submitting, routing, or confirming them. Staff coordinate manually with the Capitol Visitor Center and other offices by phone and email, and requests are easy to lose or duplicate. Each office builds its own tracking method from scratch.
rows.Solution Statement: Build a shared constituent tour request tool
rows.Solution Description: The House develops a secure online tool where staff submit and track constituent tour requests, coordinate scheduling with the Capitol Visitor Center, and confirm requests directly with constituents. Offices no longer rely on ad hoc phone and email coordination for a routine, recurring task.
rows.Horizon Justification: It replaces an informal workaround with a shared tool but does not change how tours are scheduled, staffed, or resourced, so the underlying coordination burden remains.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 177: Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: TourTracker is widely used by member offices but requires offices to purchase it. CHA and CAO are exploring an enterprise-wide solution.
rows.Concerns: The tool organizes tour requests but adds no capacity at the Capitol Visitor Center itself, so the number of tours a constituent can actually get stays capped by the same scheduling bottleneck as before.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 177

rows.Problem Statement: Constituent flag requests are tracked with no efficient process
rows.Problem Description: Offices process requests from constituents for flags flown over the Capitol, a high volume, recurring constituent service. Without a dedicated system, staff manage requests, verify eligibility, and coordinate delivery by hand, so the process takes time disproportionate to its complexity. Each office manages it differently.
rows.Solution Statement: Develop a shared flag request tracking process
rows.Solution Description: The House builds a more efficient process, potentially a shared tool, for offices to submit, track, and fulfill constituent flag requests, from intake through delivery confirmation. This frees staff time currently spent on manual tracking of a routine request type.
rows.Horizon Justification: It streamlines an existing manual workflow without changing who owns flag requests or how the underlying service is delivered.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 178: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The FlagTrack program developed by the House Digital Service is now live. 119th Congress: The Subcommittee requested Modernization Initiatives Account funds for additions.
rows.Concerns: A shared tracking tool speeds up intake and status checks but does not touch the physical work of sourcing and delivering flags, so the time saved applies only to the paperwork half of the request.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 178

rows.Problem Statement: Offices cannot measure their own constituent service quality
rows.Problem Description: Congressional offices provide constituent services, casework, tours, flag requests, and more, but have no standard way to survey or track how constituents experience that service. Without data, offices cannot identify where service is breaking down or compare performance over time. No tool for this exists at the institutional level.
rows.Solution Statement: Provide optional constituent service experience surveys
rows.Solution Description: The House develops and offers offices optional tools for surveying and tracking constituents' customer service experience. Offices that opt in gain data on response times, satisfaction, and service gaps they can use to improve casework and constituent services; participation and use of the resulting data remain up to each office.
rows.Horizon Justification: The tool is voluntary, and offices that do not opt in continue operating exactly as before, so the reform adds capability without changing how constituent service is measured or governed.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 179: Closed-Resolved. 117th Congress: Need to offer a Customer Experience package that offices can opt into to solicit feedback from constituents at the end of an interaction.
rows.Concerns: Participation is voluntary, so the offices with the weakest constituent service, the ones this tool would help identify, are also the least likely to opt in and expose that gap through the data.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 179

rows.Problem Statement: The Capitol Visitor Center tour is generic and impersonal
rows.Problem Description: Capitol Visitor Center tours are largely generic and group based, and give constituents little sense of who represents them or how their opinions translate into House votes. The tour does not connect a visitor's district or interests to the member who represents them or to specific legislative action. Past exhibit and technology upgrades have not addressed this gap.
rows.Solution Statement: Personalize and add interactivity to Capitol Visitor Center tours
rows.Solution Description: Future Capitol Visitor Center upgrades add personalized, interactive elements so constituents can look up their own representative, see how that member voted on issues the constituent cares about, and understand how their input is reflected in House action. The tour becomes a tool for public understanding of representation rather than a static walkthrough.
rows.Horizon Justification: The upgrade improves what one exhibit shows visitors but is a one-time capital project tied to a single renovation cycle; it does not create a standing mechanism connecting constituents to legislative action beyond the visit itself.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 180: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The Capitol Visitor Center now offers a number of interactive displays and educational activities for visitors.
rows.Concerns: The interactive upgrade is tied to a single renovation cycle rather than a recurring budget line, so the personalized content is current the day it opens and ages as votes and representatives change until the next capital project refreshes it.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 180

rows.Additional Tags: In-House Development, Professional Development, Coordination, Operations
rows.Problem Statement: Technology education efforts reach few staff and do not scale
rows.Problem Description: The Congressional Hackathon and similar one-off events introduce staff to new technology and prototyping, but they are episodic rather than institutionalized. There is no standing program that builds technical fluency across the House workforce, so participation depends on staff opportunistically finding a single annual event. Momentum from each event dissipates once it ends.
rows.Solution Statement: Institutionalize and expand technology education programs
rows.Solution Description: Congress establishes standing technology education and innovation programming, building on and expanding events like the Congressional Hackathon into a recurring, resourced program rather than a one-off. Staff gain ongoing access to technology training and prototyping opportunities instead of a single annual event.
rows.Horizon Justification: Institutionalizing turns a one-off event into a standing, funded program the institution owns and repeats on its own schedule, rather than one that depends on a single annual event reappearing.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 181: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: In September 2023 Speaker McCarthy, Leader Jeffries, and the CAO held the Congressional Hackathon 5.0. CAO participation moved this to fully implemented.
rows.Concerns: Turning the Hackathon into a standing program means a recurring staff and budget line inside the Legislative Branch appropriation that does not exist today, and formalizing it risks losing the informal energy that made the one-off event work.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 181

rows.Problem Statement: Mature, widely used technology never becomes official House infrastructure
rows.Problem Description: Technology tools can reach wide adoption inside the House, becoming essential to how offices operate, without ever being formally institutionalized. There is no defined process for moving a tool from ad hoc, office-level use to supported, institution-owned infrastructure, so tools offices already depend on remain informal and vulnerable to loss of support or continuity.
rows.Solution Statement: Create an onboarding process for mature House technology
rows.Solution Description: The House establishes a formal onboarding process that identifies technology reaching a mature stage of development or wide, essential use and moves it into institutional ownership and support. Tools offices already depend on gain the same maintenance, security review, and continuity that officially adopted systems receive.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates a standing, repeatable process the CAO owns for absorbing mature tools into institutional infrastructure, rather than a one-time review or pilot.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 182: Open-In Progress. 117th Congress: Need to develop an onboarding process for mature House technology, allowing off-ramping of obsolete technology.
rows.Concerns: The CAO decides what counts as mature enough to adopt, a judgment call that can favor tools with institutional sponsors over ones staff actually use most, and taking ownership adds an ongoing maintenance and security cost the CAO carries indefinitely.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 182

rows.Additional Tags: In-House Development, Data, Transparency, Rules, CAO
rows.Problem Statement: House-built software is released to the public only case by case
rows.Problem Description: The House already requires public release of some tools built on public, non-sensitive congressional data, but release is not the default. Digital applications the House develops for its own use are not systematically opened as source code, so outside developers, researchers, and other legislatures cannot build on House-developed work unless a case is made for each release.
rows.Solution Statement: Make House-developed applications open source by default
rows.Solution Description: House-developed digital applications are released as open source by default rather than through case-by-case requests, with exceptions only where security or sensitivity requires them. Outside developers, researchers, and other legislatures can inspect, reuse, and build on House-built code without petitioning for access.
rows.Horizon Justification: Setting a default changes the institution's standing policy rather than releasing one dataset or tool, and it holds without renewal once written into practice.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 183: Closed-Resolved. 118th Congress: Though the initial intention was to open-source all House-developed digital products, CAO determined this code would have limited value.
rows.Concerns: The security and sensitivity exceptions are undefined, so an agency can classify code as sensitive to avoid release, and the default proves easy to route around in practice.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 183

rows.Problem Statement: House and Senate technology standards diverge without coordination
rows.Problem Description: The House and Senate develop technology standards and processes largely independently, from data formats to procurement practices. This duplication means tools and data built in one chamber often cannot interoperate with the other, and each chamber solves problems the other has already solved. No formal mechanism pushes the two chambers toward common standards.
rows.Solution Statement: Align House and Senate technology standards
rows.Solution Description: The House and Senate work together to align their technology standards and processes where it makes sense, from data formats to security review, reducing duplicate effort and improving interoperability. Staff and vendors face fewer chamber-specific requirements for tools meant to serve the whole institution.
rows.Horizon Justification: Alignment work depends on continued cooperation between two independently governed chambers and can stall without a shared body enforcing it, so it relieves duplication without creating a single owner of the standard.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 184: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The House and Senate have connected Office 365 systems to allow better document sharing. The CIO and CIS counsels meet regularly.
rows.Concerns: Alignment depends on voluntary cooperation between two independently governed chambers with no shared authority to enforce it, so standards can converge on paper while implementation drifts apart again.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 184

rows.Problem Statement: Vendors lack visibility into how House technology approval works
rows.Problem Description: Potential technology vendors have little public information about House requirements, review criteria, or how to begin the approval and onboarding process. Vendors often build products against assumptions about what the House needs and discover actual requirements only after starting review, which wastes vendor effort and slows the pipeline from both directions.
rows.Solution Statement: Publish vendor information and streamline approval
rows.Solution Description: The House publishes clearer public information for potential technology vendors, covering requirements, review criteria, and the approval and onboarding process, and streamlines that process so vendors that meet the bar move through faster. Vendors can assess fit before investing in a full proposal, and offices see a wider, better-prepared vendor pool.
rows.Horizon Justification: It publishes more information and speeds an existing review process rather than creating a new institutional structure to manage vendor relationships going forward.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 185: Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: The Subcommittee held two roundtables during the 118th Congress and is engaged with the CAO on improving the vendor approval process.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 39 (tracker Rec 20): Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: The House has made progress reforming this process for cloud-based vendors. Subcommittee is continuing to work with CAO to examine opportunities to reform the process for all technology vendors.
rows.Concerns: Clearer public rules invite scrutiny of who already gets fast-tracked, and the offices that benefit from an opaque process have little incentive to expose how it actually works.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 185

rows.Problem Statement: The House has no formal program for recurring technology vendors
rows.Problem Description: Some technology vendors work with the House repeatedly, but there is no established program that recognizes or streamlines this relationship. Each new engagement with a familiar vendor still runs through the full review process, and the CAO has no structured way to build a bench of pre-vetted delivery partners.
rows.Solution Statement: Establish a CAO Established Delivery Partners program
rows.Solution Description: The CAO creates an Established Delivery Partners program for digital solution vendors that work regularly with the House, giving pre-vetted vendors a faster path through future engagements. The CAO builds and maintains a standing bench of trusted vendors rather than re-evaluating the same vendors from scratch each time.
rows.Horizon Justification: It creates a standing, CAO-owned program with defined criteria for vendor status, so it persists and accumulates value beyond any single procurement.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 186: Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: The Subcommittee is currently engaged with the CAO on developing this program and establishing guidelines.
rows.Concerns: A standing bench of pre-vetted vendors risks becoming a closed list that favors incumbents, narrowing the field for newer or smaller firms that could otherwise underbid on a given contract.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 186

rows.Problem Statement: House policy discourages using outside civic technology software
rows.Problem Description: Outside civic technology organizations build software useful to congressional offices, but House policy does not clearly address when staff can use it or draw on its underlying code. Existing gift rule guidance covers open-source contribution narrowly; broader use of civic tech software remains uncertain, so offices default to avoiding it.
rows.Solution Statement: Review House policy on civic technology software use
rows.Solution Description: The House reviews its current policies and, where appropriate, creates clear opportunities for congressional use of software, including its underlying code, developed by outside civic technology organizations. Offices gain a defined, permitted path to adopt civic tech tools instead of an unclear one that defaults to no.
rows.Horizon Justification: A policy review may recommend new rules, but the review itself is a one-time assessment and does not by itself establish an ongoing mechanism for approving civic tech software.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 187: Closed-Resolved. 119th Congress: Subcommittee staff consulted the House Ethics Committee on whether accepting open-source code would constitute a gift violation.
rows.Concerns: The review is a single assessment with no mechanism guaranteeing it leads to new rules, so offices can still lack a defined path to adopt civic tech tools once the review concludes.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 187

rows.Problem Statement: No one coordinates priorities across House digital infrastructure
rows.Problem Description: House digital infrastructure, systems, tools, and platforms across offices and support agencies, is maintained and developed without a single body setting priorities across it. Individual offices and support agencies make infrastructure decisions largely in isolation, so investment and maintenance are uncoordinated at the institutional level.
rows.Solution Statement: Establish a digital infrastructure working group
rows.Solution Description: The House establishes a high-level working group to prioritize and coordinate the maintenance and development of its digital infrastructure across offices and support agencies. Infrastructure decisions previously made in isolation get a shared venue for sequencing and tradeoffs.
rows.Horizon Justification: A working group can set informal priorities but holds no formal authority or budget of its own, so infrastructure decisions still ultimately rest with the separate bodies it coordinates rather than with the group itself.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 188: Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need a coordinated working group of leadership offices, relevant committees, support offices, and outside advisors to prioritize digital infrastructure.
rows.Concerns: The working group has no budget or binding authority, so support agencies with competing priorities can simply decline to follow its sequencing, leaving coordination voluntary rather than real.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 188

rows.Problem Statement: The House Digital Service has no venue to set priorities
rows.Problem Description: House Administration created the House Digital Service to build shared technology for member offices, but nothing outside the service itself weighs in on what it builds first. Priorities are set internally, without input from the members and committees the service is meant to serve.
rows.Solution Statement: Create a Digital Service Advisory Board
rows.Solution Description: Stand up an advisory board, drawn from members, committee staff, and technical experts, to review the Digital Service's roadmap and weigh in on what it prioritizes. The board has no operational authority of its own; it structures input into decisions the service already makes.
rows.Horizon Justification: The board only advises. It does not change who controls the Digital Service or give it independent authority to act across the House, so the underlying reach and reporting problems remain.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 189: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The Board and HDS Advisory Group has launched with 358 members. All staff can join regardless of seniority.
rows.Concerns: An advisory board with no operational authority does not resolve who the Digital Service reports to or how far its reach extends, so the service is free to set its recommendations aside.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 189

rows.Problem Statement: Callers reach House offices with no identifying information passed along
rows.Problem Description: The Capitol switchboard routes constituent calls to House offices but strips out caller information in the process, so staff who answer know nothing about who is calling or why until the constituent explains it themselves. The switchboard technology has not been updated to carry that information through.
rows.Solution Statement: Modernize the Capitol switchboard to pass caller information through
rows.Solution Description: Update the switchboard so caller information collected when a call comes in is passed along to the receiving House office rather than dropped. Staff answering the phone see who is calling before they pick up, the same way any modern office phone system works.
rows.Horizon Justification: This upgrades one piece of shared phone infrastructure. It does not change who operates the switchboard or give offices any new control over their own call data, so the system stays as centralized and dependent on outside upgrades as before.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 190: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The Capitol Switchboard now shares caller ID information across chambers.
rows.Concerns: This is a narrow fix to shared infrastructure that leaves the switchboard's centralized operation and any underlying vendor contract unchanged, so offices gain caller ID but no say over the system itself.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 190

rows.Problem Statement: Committees produce hearing records by hand, one committee at a time
rows.Problem Description: Each committee manages its own hearing records, from transcripts to witness materials, without a shared process or system. GPO has the printing and archiving expertise to standardize this but has not been asked to build a common process, so committees duplicate the same manual work independently.
rows.Solution Statement: GPO builds a standard hearing records automation process
rows.Solution Description: Direct GPO to design and offer committees a standard automated process for producing and archiving hearing records. Committees that adopt it spend less staff time assembling records by hand, and records end up in a more consistent, searchable format.
rows.Horizon Justification: GPO offers the process rather than requiring it, so adoption is voluntary and committees can keep working the old way. The underlying committee by committee ownership of hearing records does not change.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 191: Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: This is part of the Clerk's Roadmap for Publishing Legislative Documents in USLM XML Format, which includes 10 stages.
rows.Concerns: GPO can only offer the process, not require it, so committees attached to their existing workflow can decline, and the labor-intensive, committee-by-committee production the reform targets continues unchanged.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 191

rows.Problem Statement: Members and staff rarely know what Legislative Counsel can do for them
rows.Problem Description: The House Office of the Legislative Counsel already runs education and outreach to make members and staff aware of its drafting services, but the effort is under resourced relative to the office's caseload. Awareness stays low because outreach depends on capacity the office does not consistently have.
rows.Solution Statement: Fund HOLC's outreach and education efforts
rows.Solution Description: Provide dedicated resources so the Legislative Counsel's office can expand the trainings, briefings, and proactive outreach it already runs for members and staff. More offices learn what drafting support is available and how to request it.
rows.Horizon Justification: This funds more of an existing outreach effort rather than changing how members and staff learn about or access Legislative Counsel's services, so the underlying discovery problem persists once the added resources are spent.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 193: Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: HOLC needs resources to add employees focused on proactive outreach to member and committee offices.
rows.Concerns: This funds more of the same outreach model rather than changing how members learn services exist, so awareness rises temporarily after new trainings but fades again as staff turn over.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 193

rows.Problem Statement: New members and staff do not know what support offices offer
rows.Problem Description: Members and staff learn about House business support offices, such as the CAO and the Clerk, mostly by accident, through word of mouth or by stumbling into a problem the office happens to solve. There is no regular moment when those offices introduce themselves directly to a new Congress.
rows.Solution Statement: Hold a term-start Open-House with business support offices
rows.Solution Description: At the start of each Congress, have House business support offices and agencies host an in-person Open-House where members and staff can meet the people and services behind each office. Offices get a direct channel to introduce what they offer before staff hit a problem that sends them looking.
rows.Horizon Justification: The Open-House happens once per Congress and depends on offices showing up and staff attending. It raises awareness at a single moment without changing how staff discover or access services the rest of the term.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 194: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: A support office open house was included as part of New Member Orientation; the Longworth Main Street Project includes a corridor of public-facing offices.
rows.Concerns: The event happens once per Congress and only reaches staff who choose to attend, so it raises awareness at a single moment without giving offices an ongoing way to be found later.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 194

rows.Problem Statement: No record tracks how much time members spend voting late
rows.Problem Description: Votes have an allotted time window, but the House does not publish any cumulative accounting of how much time individual members spend voting after it closes. Without a public record, there is no visible pressure on the behavior and no way to see whether it is getting better or worse.
rows.Solution Statement: Publish a regular late-voting report
rows.Solution Description: Have the House publish a regular report showing the cumulative time each member has spent voting after the allotted window closes. The report gives the public and leadership a standing record to point to, where none currently exists.
rows.Horizon Justification: Publishing the report creates visibility but no enforcement mechanism. Members who vote late face no formal consequence, so the underlying behavior can continue unchanged even after the report exists.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 197: Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need regular reporting from the electronic voting system noting the total time individual members voted outside the time allotted.
rows.Concerns: Publishing the report creates reputational pressure but no penalty, so members who tolerate the political cost keep voting late, and the report also flags members with legitimate scheduling conflicts alongside habitual latecomers.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 197

rows.Problem Statement: Committees rarely study how other legislatures solve the same problems
rows.Problem Description: Committee members build relationships and expertise mostly within their own chamber and party, with few structured opportunities to see how other national legislatures handle similar institutional problems. Existing travel is ad hoc and rarely framed around bipartisan learning.
rows.Solution Statement: Run semi-regular bipartisan international CODELs
rows.Solution Description: Have the Committee on House Administration and the Committee on Rules jointly organize semi-regular, bipartisan delegations to study how other legislatures operate. Members return with concrete comparisons and, because the trips are bipartisan, with working relationships across party lines that carry back into committee work.
rows.Horizon Justification: Participation is voluntary and depends on which members choose to travel, so the trips build relationships without changing how committees are structured or staffed. Nothing requires what members learn abroad to change committee practice at home.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 198: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The Select Committee and CHA have participated in CODELs that included sessions focused on modernization.
rows.Concerns: CODELs draw public criticism as travel junkets, and because participation and follow-through are voluntary, nothing compels the committees to act on what members bring back.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 198

rows.Problem Statement: New member orientation ends before members are ready to use it
rows.Problem Description: Current orientation is compressed into the first days of a new Congress, when new members are overwhelmed and retain little of what they are told. Nothing brings them back later, once they have enough experience on the job to know what questions to ask.
rows.Solution Statement: Offer a bipartisan seminar later in the first year
rows.Solution Description: Have the Committee on House Administration offer new members a voluntary, bipartisan update seminar well after orientation ends, once they have been on the job long enough to have real questions. The seminar reinforces material from orientation and covers what members did not yet know to ask about.
rows.Horizon Justification: The seminar is a voluntary, one-time add-on to a fixed orientation window. It supplements the existing orientation model rather than restructuring how or when orientation content is delivered across the term.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 199: Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need to build on New Member Orientation to provide a follow-up opportunity for new members after having served several months.
rows.Concerns: The seminar is a voluntary add-on layered onto a fixed orientation calendar rather than a redesign of it, so members who most need the later material can simply skip an optional session.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 199

rows.Problem Statement: Member travel reimbursement rules do not match standard business practice
rows.Problem Description: House rules governing travel related reimbursement for members were written separately from, and have not kept pace with, the standard business travel practices used across the private sector and the rest of the federal government. Members and their offices navigate a reimbursement process that is stricter or more confusing than the norm elsewhere, and travel expenditures are not tracked or reported in a way that supports accountability and transparency.
rows.Solution Statement: Align member travel reimbursement with standard practice and improve transparency
rows.Solution Description: Rewrite House rules on member travel related expense reimbursement to match standard business travel practices used in the private sector and elsewhere in the federal government, and update travel expenditure policies to improve efficiency and strengthen accountability and transparency in how travel funds are tracked and reported. Members and offices follow the same kind of reimbursement process used everywhere else, rather than a House-specific variant.
rows.Horizon Justification: Once the rule is rewritten it applies going forward without further action or funding, so the change is durable and does not depend on any office choosing to opt in.
rows.Current Status (Optional):
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 200: Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: CHA updated the Members' Handbook to include language and regulations allowing member reimbursement for travel expenses.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 51 (tracker Rec 38): Closed-Resolved. 117th Congress: Existing travel expenditure policies allow for more modern travel transactions as part of the House Travel Card Program.
rows.Concerns: Rewriting reimbursement rules to match private sector practice reads publicly as members loosening rules on their own expenses, inviting the same scrutiny that has slowed past attempts to touch member travel accounts.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 200

rows.Problem Statement: Modernization work has no permanent committee to live in
rows.Problem Description: Ongoing modernization work has depended on temporary select committees that expire and must be re-authorized from scratch. Between select committees, no standing committee is responsible for institutional improvement, so momentum and staff expertise built up during one select committee's life does not automatically carry forward.
rows.Solution Statement: House a Modernization Subcommittee inside House Administration
rows.Solution Description: Create a standing Modernization Subcommittee within the Committee on House Administration, giving institutional improvement work a permanent committee home rather than a temporary select committee that has to be re-created and re-staffed each time. The subcommittee carries modernization work forward between select committees rather than losing it when one expires.
rows.Horizon Justification: The subcommittee is a standing structure created within House rules rather than a body that expires and requires re-authorization, so modernization work has a permanent institutional home even when no select committee is active.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 201: Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: The Modernization Subcommittee was formed under CHA at the start of the 118th Congress.
rows.Concerns: A subcommittee still answers to House Administration's chair and competes with that committee's other priorities for staff and floor time, so modernization work gains a permanent address but not guaranteed attention.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 201

rows.Problem Statement: Select committees on modernization lapse and are not reliably renewed
rows.Problem Description: The Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress has existed only when the House chose to re-authorize it, most recently after a gap with no committee working on institutional improvement at all. Nothing requires the House to stand one up again, so the work depends on each new Congress choosing to restart it.
rows.Solution Statement: Require a Modernization Select Committee every fourth Congress
rows.Solution Description: Adopt a standing House rule requiring authorization of a Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress at least once every four Congresses. Modernization work resumes on a predictable schedule instead of depending on whether a given Congress chooses to revive it.
rows.Horizon Justification: The recurring authorization requirement is written into House rules, so it persists and triggers automatically on a fixed schedule rather than depending on a fresh decision by each new Congress.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), Rec 202: Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need the House, with or without the Senate, to authorize a Select Committee with a mandate to evaluate the institution at more regular intervals.
rows.Concerns: A future majority can waive or ignore the requirement the same way earlier modernization panels lapsed without renewal, and even a guaranteed committee still needs staff and expertise rebuilt each time it is re-created.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 117-646 (Dec. 2022), Rec. 202

rows.Problem Statement: Lobbying disclosure filings are scattered and hard to search
rows.Problem Description: Lobbyists file disclosure reports with the Clerk of the House and the Secretary of the Senate, but the two systems are separate, not linked, and use inconsistent formats. A citizen or reporter who wants to know who is lobbying on a given bill has no single place to search and must cross-reference databases that were never built to talk to each other.
rows.Solution Statement: Consolidate and standardize public lobbying disclosure data
rows.Solution Description: Merge House and Senate lobbying disclosure filings into one standardized, searchable, machine-readable database linked to the bills and issues lobbyists report working on. The public, press, and Congress can then search who is lobbying on a topic in one place instead of checking two separate systems.
rows.Horizon Justification: A unified disclosure database is a permanent public record system the institution maintains going forward, not a one-time release.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 3 (tracker Rec 3): Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: Acting Clerk McCumber testified before CHA that his office is working with the Senate to develop a new lobbying disclosure system.
rows.Concerns: Merging House and Senate systems requires two independently governed chambers to agree on one data standard and fund a joint database, and firms that currently sell lobbying compliance tools have reason to resist a shared public alternative.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 3

rows.Problem Statement: Expired agency and program authorizations go unnoticed by Congress
rows.Problem Description: Authorizations for federal agencies and programs lapse on schedules tracked nowhere in one place, so members and staff have no simple way to see which authorizations have expired and need attention. Committees identify lapses program by program, often years after expiration, because no dashboard consolidates the information across the government.
rows.Solution Statement: One-click dashboard of expired authorizations
rows.Solution Description: Build a single dashboard, drawing on existing CRS and CBO tracking, that shows in one click which agencies and programs are operating on expired authorizations. Committees and members can use it to prioritize reauthorization work instead of discovering lapses individually.
rows.Horizon Justification: It is a lookup tool layered on existing tracking data, not a change to how authorizations are set, reviewed, or enforced.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 4 (tracker Rec 4): Closed-Not Implemented. 118th Congress: Both CBO and CRS report challenges to creating a complete, authoritative list. CBO currently produces an annual report covering only expired and expiring authorizations.
rows.Concerns: The dashboard surfaces lapses that committees have often left unaddressed for reasons of political convenience, and visibility alone does not compel reauthorization, so expired programs can sit flagged indefinitely.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 4

rows.Problem Statement: Committee vote records are hard to find and compare
rows.Problem Description: Committees must disclose how members vote on amendments and motions in markup, but the records sit on individual committee websites in inconsistent formats, some as scanned images of paper tallies. A reporter or constituent who wants to see how a member voted in committee has no single, searchable source and must check each committee separately.
rows.Solution Statement: One-click public committee vote lookup
rows.Solution Description: Build a single, searchable interface, drawing on committees' existing disclosure obligation, that shows with one click how any member voted on any committee markup or amendment. It aggregates records committees already produce rather than creating a new reporting requirement.
rows.Horizon Justification: It packages existing committee disclosure records into a shared interface without changing what committees must record or how.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 5 (tracker Rec 5): Open-In Progress. 119th Congress: Construction of the Committee Activity Portal has developed its initial three modules: Committee Vote, Committee Referral, and Committee Membership.
rows.Concerns: Making committee votes easy to browse increases political exposure for members who currently benefit from those votes being hard to compile, giving them reason to resist a tool that surfaces patterns interest groups can use in campaigns.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 5

rows.Problem Statement: Congressional caucus membership and activity are not published
rows.Problem Description: Members form Congressional Member Organizations, informal caucuses that shape policy positions and coordinate votes, but no current public list exists of which caucuses are active, who chairs them, or who belongs. The Committee on House Administration keeps internal registration records, but nothing requires publishing them on a recurring basis.
rows.Solution Statement: Annual public list of active member organizations
rows.Solution Description: Require the Committee on House Administration to publish, once a year, the roster of registered Congressional Member Organizations along with their leadership and membership. The public and press gain a standing, current record of caucus activity instead of having to request it.
rows.Horizon Justification: A recurring, rule-based publication requirement is a standing institutional practice rather than a one-time disclosure.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 6 (tracker Rec 72): Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: CHA has updated the list of CMOs but has not included a list of ECMOs.
rows.Concerns: The value depends on caucuses reporting membership and leadership accurately, and because there is no independent verification, an organization with reason to obscure its activity can file a thin or incomplete roster.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 6

rows.Problem Statement: Staff have no single place to get HR help
rows.Problem Description: Personal office, committee, and leadership staff handle benefits, payroll questions, and workplace policy issues by contacting whatever office or contact they can find, since no service is built for how the House actually employs them. Each office effectively works out its own way to handle routine personnel questions.
rows.Solution Statement: One-stop human resources hub for Hill staff
rows.Solution Description: Establish a dedicated HR hub inside the CAO that serves Member, committee, and leadership staff through one point of contact for benefits, payroll, and personnel policy questions. Staff get consistent answers, and offices stop building their own workarounds for routine HR needs.
rows.Horizon Justification: A dedicated, permanent HR office is a standing institutional service rather than a temporary fix.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 11 (tracker Rec 6): Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: Pursuant to H. Res. 756, CAO announced in August 2021 the creation of a House Human Resources Hub. It is now live and accessible to congressional staff.
rows.Concerns: A centralized HR hub asks Member offices to route sensitive personnel matters through the CAO, and offices that value discretion over their own hiring and firing have reason to keep managing HR themselves.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 11

rows.Problem Statement: Diversity and inclusion work in the House has no permanent home
rows.Problem Description: The House Office of Diversity and Inclusion operates on a temporary basis, renewed each Congress rather than fixed in the rules, so its programs, staff, and relationships with offices can lapse at any transition. Offices cannot count on continuity in the recruitment, retention, or training support tied to the office.
rows.Solution Statement: Make the Office of Diversity and Inclusion permanent
rows.Solution Description: Establish the office in House rules as a permanent entity rather than a standing order renewed each Congress. Its recruitment, retention, and training programs then continue automatically across Congresses instead of depending on reauthorization.
rows.Horizon Justification: Permanent rules-based status makes the office self-sustaining rather than dependent on renewal each Congress.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 12 (tracker Rec 7): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The FY24 Legislative Branch Appropriations Act reduced ODI funding to zero. Many of its duties, responsibilities, and staff were rolled into an office within CAO.
rows.Concerns: Rules are rewritten at the start of every Congress, so a future majority hostile to the office's mission can strip its permanent status just as easily, and getting there requires a floor vote on a politically charged office.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 12

rows.Problem Statement: House staff are paid monthly while most employers pay biweekly
rows.Problem Description: The House payroll system pays staff once a month, unlike the semimonthly or biweekly schedules common at nearly every other employer, which strains staff living paycheck to paycheck and makes House jobs less attractive next to comparable outside pay. Changing the schedule requires reworking legacy payroll infrastructure the House has not prioritized.
rows.Solution Statement: Study moving House payroll to semimonthly pay
rows.Solution Description: Direct the CAO to examine what it would take to convert the House payroll system from monthly to semimonthly disbursement, including system costs and an implementation timeline. The study produces a concrete cost and feasibility assessment rather than committing to the change itself.
rows.Horizon Justification: It commissions a feasibility study, not the payroll system change itself.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 13 (tracker Rec 8): Closed-Not Implemented. 119th Congress: Pursuant to H. Res. 756, CAO completed a suitability review in November 2020 and commissioned a comprehensive study in 2024 on moving the House to semimonthly pay.
rows.Concerns: Feasibility studies commissioned without a mandate to act often get shelved once the cost estimate comes back, so the study can conclude the change is worthwhile and payroll still stays on the old monthly cycle.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 13

rows.Problem Statement: Member office staff caps limit how many people offices can hire
rows.Problem Description: House rules cap the number of permanent and additional staff a Member office may employ, a limit set decades ago that has not kept pace with the volume of casework, legislative work, and constituent communication offices now handle. Offices that need more capacity cannot add staff even when they have the budget authority to pay them.
rows.Solution Statement: Raise the Member office staff cap
rows.Solution Description: Increase the maximum number of permanent and additional staff a Member office may employ. Offices gain the ability to hire more people as workload grows, instead of staying capped regardless of budget or need.
rows.Horizon Justification: A higher cap is a standing rules change that persists across Congresses rather than a temporary allowance.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 14 (tracker Rec 9): Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Pursuant to H. Res. 756, the House Office of Inspector General completed a review in December 2021 and recommended increasing the cap; needs CHA action.
rows.Concerns: A higher cap only helps offices that also have the budget to pay more staff, so without a matching increase in the Members' Representational Allowance the change mostly benefits offices that already have room in their accounts.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 14

rows.Problem Statement: Constituent communications costs compete with staff salaries in office budgets
rows.Problem Description: Member offices pay for franked mail, newsletters, and other constituent communications out of the same Members' Representational Allowance that funds staff salaries, so heavier communications needs directly reduce what an office can spend on people. Offices with active communications operations trade staffing capacity for outreach as a result.
rows.Solution Statement: Shared account for constituent communications costs
rows.Solution Description: Remove constituent communications expenses from the Members' Representational Allowance and fund them instead through a separate, shared institutional account. Office budgets are freed to focus on staff salaries and operating costs, while communications spending is tracked and funded centrally.
rows.Horizon Justification: A separate, standing funding account is a permanent change to how the institution budgets, not a one-time transfer.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 18 (tracker Rec 65): Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need a policy change, and perhaps a statutory solution, to create a separate account for constituent communications costs.
rows.Concerns: Removing communications costs from the MRA takes away the budget tradeoff that currently disciplines mailing and newsletter volume, and the new shared account still needs its own funding line inside the legislative branch appropriation.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 18

https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: Congressional staff have limited access to health insurance options
rows.Problem Description: Congressional staff, particularly those in district offices, part-time roles, or lower pay bands, have historically faced narrower health insurance options and eligibility rules than staff in comparable federal or private sector jobs. Gaps in coverage make congressional employment less competitive against other offers.
rows.Solution Statement: Expand health insurance access for congressional staff
rows.Solution Description: Broaden eligibility and options for health insurance coverage across House employment categories, including district and part-time staff. Staff gain benefits closer to what comparable employers offer, and offices compete for talent on more even footing.
rows.Horizon Justification: Expanded benefits eligibility is a permanent policy change built into how the institution employs staff.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 21 (tracker Rec 68): Closed-Resolved. 119th Congress: Each Member, Chair, and Leader can designate their staff to either DCHL or FEHB health plans based on their interpretation of the Affordable Care Act.
rows.Concerns: Expanded eligibility for district and part-time staff raises the institution's aggregate benefits cost, and the reform names no funding source, so the expansion competes with member office budgets or a separate appropriation for staff pay.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 21

rows.Problem Statement: District office lease costs and terms vary with no central negotiation
rows.Problem Description: Each House district office negotiates its own commercial lease independently, so rental rates and terms vary widely across offices even in similar markets, and no one in the House brings comparative leverage or market data to individual negotiations. The CAO tracks lease payments but does not actively negotiate on offices' behalf.
rows.Solution Statement: Centralize district office lease negotiation practices
rows.Solution Description: Have the CAO develop and apply a standard practice for negotiating district office leases, using comparative rental data across offices to secure more consistent rates. Offices gain institutional leverage and market knowledge instead of negotiating alone.
rows.Horizon Justification: A negotiation practice improves outcomes within the current system of office-by-office leasing rather than restructuring how district office space is acquired.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 26 (tracker Rec 94): Closed-Not Implemented. 117th Congress: Select Committee staff have held discussions with GSA; needs CHA to develop a system for managing district office leases separately from individual offices.
rows.Concerns: A standard negotiating practice at the CAO builds leverage but leaves each office negotiating its own lease individually; landlords in tight markets can ignore comparative data since the practice creates no binding centralized authority.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 26

rows.Problem Statement: Newly elected Members have no dedicated help setting up their office
rows.Problem Description: A Member-elect must build a staff, set up payroll and systems, and open a Washington office in the weeks between election and swearing-in, without any staff of their own to help. Everything falls to the Member-elect personally or to campaign staff unfamiliar with House administrative systems.
rows.Solution Statement: Authorize a paid transition staff hire for Members-elect
rows.Solution Description: Let newly elected Members hire and pay one transition staff member during the period between election and taking office. That person can begin office setup, hiring, and administrative work before the Member is sworn in.
rows.Horizon Justification: The hiring authority is a standing rule available to every incoming Member going forward, not a one-time accommodation.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 27 (tracker Rec 11): Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 provided funding for the cost of hiring transition staff.
rows.Concerns: One paid hire for a few pre-swearing-in weeks is a narrow fix; it does not extend to office space, budget for a full staff, or the other transition costs a Member-elect faces before taking office.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 27
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562/pdf/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562.pdf
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: Members receive no required cybersecurity training
rows.Problem Description: Member offices handle sensitive constituent data, legislative strategy, and internal communications, yet Members themselves face no requirement to learn basic cybersecurity practice. Training exists for staff in some offices, but attendance depends on the office, and Members are rarely included. A single compromised account can expose an entire office's correspondence and casework files.
rows.Solution Statement: Mandatory cybersecurity training for Members
rows.Solution Description: Require every Member to complete cybersecurity training on a set schedule, delivered through the House's existing security and IT training infrastructure. Completion becomes a standing condition of office rather than an optional briefing, so awareness of phishing, credential hygiene, and device security holds across turnover.
rows.Horizon Justification: The requirement is written into House rules and administered on a recurring basis, so it persists on its own once adopted rather than depending on a single briefing or pilot.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 32 (tracker Rec 16): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: Cybersecurity training is included in New Member Orientation and is categorized as mandatory.
rows.Concerns: Members writing a training mandate for themselves raises a compliance question: who tracks completion and what happens when a Member skips it. Training also addresses awareness, not the weak account and vendor security practices that cause most breaches.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 32
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562/pdf/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562.pdf
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: House floor and committee broadcasts lack closed captioning
rows.Problem Description: House proceedings are streamed and archived without closed captions, so deaf and hard of hearing constituents, staff, and researchers cannot follow debate or committee testimony without a separate transcript, which often lags the event by days. Existing broadcast infrastructure was not built with captioning as a standard output.
rows.Solution Statement: Require closed captioning on all House broadcasts
rows.Solution Description: Build closed captioning into the standard workflow for every broadcast of House floor and committee proceedings, live and archived. The requirement applies across the House Recording Studio and committee broadcast systems rather than to select high-profile events.
rows.Horizon Justification: Captioning becomes a fixed requirement of the broadcast system itself, so every future proceeding is covered without a new decision each time.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 34 (tracker Rec 28): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: Nearly all committees provide some form of closed captioning for official proceedings, and the Clerk provides closed captioning for all floor proceedings.
rows.Concerns: Building captioning into every broadcast, including routine committee hearings that currently rely on ad hoc or vendor-dependent AV setups, means funding and coordinating the change across dozens of committees at once, not only high-profile floor proceedings.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 34
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562/pdf/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562.pdf
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: The Capitol complex has unmapped accessibility barriers
rows.Problem Description: No comprehensive review catalogs where the Capitol complex fails visitors, Members, and staff with disabilities, from door hardware to signage to screening procedures. Fixes happen piecemeal, driven by individual complaints rather than a full assessment of where barriers exist.
rows.Solution Statement: Comprehensive accessibility review of the Capitol complex
rows.Solution Description: Commission a review of the Capitol complex to identify accessibility barriers for people with disabilities, covering physical access, signage, and screening procedures. The review produces a prioritized list of fixes for the Architect of the Capitol and CAO to act on.
rows.Horizon Justification: A review documents where the problems are but does not itself fix a door, install signage, or change a procedure, so the barriers remain until a separate structural fix follows.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 35 (tracker Rec 29): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The Architect of the Capitol reports on accessibility barriers pursuant to the Congressional Accountability Act; in May 2024 the AOC issued a physical accessibility report.
rows.Concerns: The review only maps the barriers; the Architect of the Capitol and CAO must separately fund and execute each fix afterward, so problems documented today can sit unaddressed the way earlier piecemeal, complaint-driven fixes have.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 35
