https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: House Information Resources cannot deliver reliable IT service
rows.Problem Description: House Information Resources, the office responsible for Member office technology, is organized around legacy support structures that predate modern IT service delivery. Offices report slow response times, inconsistent service quality, and unclear escalation paths, because HIR's structure was never rebuilt around how offices actually use technology today.
rows.Solution Statement: Reorganize House Information Resources
rows.Solution Description: Restructure HIR's organization, staffing, and service model so it delivers IT support the way a modern enterprise IT department would, with clear service tiers, escalation paths, and accountability for response time. The reorganization changes how HIR is built rather than adding a program on top of it.
rows.Horizon Justification: The reform rebuilds HIR's own organizational structure, so improved service delivery is embedded in the office rather than depending on a temporary fix.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 37 (tracker Rec 18): Closed-Resolved. 118th Congress: Providing strong IT support requires ongoing attention. The CAO has worked to improve IT services; HIR now offers drop-in support and other channels.
rows.Concerns: Rebuilding HIR's structure means reassigning roles and reporting lines for existing staff, which invites internal resistance, and reorganizations of legacy IT shops often stall in execution well short of the modern service model they promise.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 37

rows.Problem Statement: HIR has no defined priority list for technology upgrades
rows.Problem Description: HIR fields technology improvement requests without a settled sense of which upgrades matter most to Member offices, so effort spreads across many small projects rather than concentrating on the fixes offices need most. Priorities shift with whichever request is loudest rather than a standing plan.
rows.Solution Statement: Direct HIR to prioritize named technology upgrades
rows.Solution Description: Require HIR to adopt a specific, ordered list of technology improvements, drawn from documented office needs, and work through it in sequence. The directive names the priorities rather than changing how HIR sets them going forward.
rows.Horizon Justification: The directive fixes today's priority list but leaves HIR's own process for setting priorities unchanged, so a new list is needed again once this one is worked through.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 38 (tracker Rec 19): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: Substantial progress continues on digitizing administrative forms, including expanded e-forms and a new employee onboarding app.
rows.Concerns: A one-time ordered list does not change how HIR sets priorities going forward, so once this list is worked through, requests again compete on whoever is loudest rather than a standing planning process.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 38
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562/pdf/GPO-CRPT-116hrpt562.pdf
https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: Member offices have no single contact for technology support
rows.Problem Description: Offices route technology requests through whichever HIR staffer happens to be available, so requests bounce between people, get answered inconsistently, and require the office to re-explain its setup each time. No one at HIR owns the full relationship with a given office.
rows.Solution Statement: Assign a dedicated HIR point of contact to each office
rows.Solution Description: Create a standing role inside HIR responsible for all technology points of contact for a given Member office, so requests reach one person who already knows that office's setup and history. The office gets continuity instead of a new contact each time.
rows.Horizon Justification: The point of contact becomes a permanent role inside HIR's organizational chart, so the interface stays fixed regardless of staff turnover.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 41 (tracker Rec 22): Closed-Resolved. 119th Congress: The CAO is addressing this via the Tech Partner Plus, Customer Advocate, and District Office Connect programs.
rows.Concerns: A dedicated point of contact is a new funded role, and routing an entire office's technology relationship through one person creates a single point of failure if that person leaves or is unavailable.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 41

https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: Members and staff have no way to rate technology vendors or HIR service
rows.Problem Description: Offices choose technology vendors and rely on HIR services with no shared record of how those vendors and services actually perform. Word of mouth between staff fills the gap, so a bad vendor can keep winning business and a strained part of HIR can go unnoticed.
rows.Solution Statement: Build a vendor and HIR service rating portal on HouseNet
rows.Solution Description: Add a portal to HouseNet where Members and staff rate and review outside technology vendors and HIR's own services. Ratings accumulate into a shared record offices can consult before choosing a vendor or escalating a complaint.
rows.Horizon Justification: The portal is a voluntary feedback tool layered on top of HIR's existing structure, so it surfaces problems without changing how HIR itself is organized or held accountable.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 42 (tracker Rec 23): Open-In Progress. 117th Congress: CAO has added features to make it easier for customers and support staff to communicate; needs systematic gauging of customer satisfaction.
rows.Concerns: Reviews are voluntary, so low participation could leave most vendors and HIR services with too few ratings to be useful, and staff may hesitate to rate HIR's own performance on a portal HIR itself hosts.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 42

https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: Offices buy technology individually at higher cost and uneven quality
rows.Problem Description: Each Member office procures its own computers, phones, and software using its own Members' Representational Allowance, so offices pay retail prices for devices that could be bought in bulk, and equipment quality varies by what each office chooses to spend. Smaller or less tech-savvy offices end up with worse equipment for the same budget.
rows.Solution Statement: CAO-provided standard technology suite at no MRA cost
rows.Solution Description: Have the CAO use the House's full purchasing volume to negotiate bulk pricing on a standard suite of current devices and software, then provide it to every office at no charge against the Members' Representational Allowance. Offices get consistent, up-to-date equipment without spending down their own budget.
rows.Horizon Justification: The CAO permanently owns bulk procurement and standard equipment provisioning, so every office benefits automatically rather than through a one-time purchase.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 43 (tracker Rec 24): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: CAO now bulk purchases technology for incoming members; full implementation would require a policy decision to create an account separate from the MRA.
rows.Concerns: Centralizing procurement at the CAO removes offices' ability to choose tools suited to specific needs and concentrates risk: one bad contract, a defective device batch, or a vendor outage now affects every office at once.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 43

rows.Problem Statement: CRS cannot turn around fact sheets at the speed of legislative action
rows.Problem Description: Congressional Research Service products typically take weeks to produce, but floor and committee schedules often move on an issue within days. Staff fall back on outside advocacy material or draft their own quick summaries because CRS's normal production timeline cannot keep pace with what is actually under consideration.
rows.Solution Statement: Prioritize a CRS rapid response fact sheet program
rows.Solution Description: Direct CRS to prioritize a rapid response track that produces short, nonpartisan fact sheets on issues and legislation currently moving in Congress, on a turnaround measured in days rather than weeks. The rest of CRS's production continues on its normal timeline.
rows.Horizon Justification: The directive asks CRS to prioritize faster output within its existing structure and staffing, so capacity for rapid response still competes with everything else CRS produces.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 44 (tracker Rec 25): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: CRS continues to increase its publication of short-form products.
rows.Concerns: The rapid response track draws on the same CRS staff and hours as everything else, so a surge in fast-turnaround requests during a busy floor period can slow both the priority track and CRS's normal production.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 44

rows.Problem Statement: Congress has not defined what a digital service function would do
rows.Problem Description: Congress has no dedicated group of technologists and designers supporting its internal and public-facing operations, and no body has formally examined what such a group would need to do, who it would serve, or how it would be structured. Proposals for a digital service circulate informally without an institutional process behind them.
rows.Solution Statement: Establish a Congressional Digital Services Task Force
rows.Solution Description: Create a task force to examine the need for a specialized group of technologists, designers, and other digital service staff supporting both the House's internal operations and its public-facing work. The task force produces findings and a recommended structure rather than standing up the service itself.
rows.Horizon Justification: The task force studies the question and reports back; it does not itself create staff positions, a budget line, or a standing office.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 46 (tracker Rec 95): Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: CAO has stood up a House Digital Service to fill this function.
rows.Concerns: A task force only studies and reports; it creates no staff positions or budget line, so a favorable recommendation can sit unimplemented unless leadership separately commits to funding the digital service it describes.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 46

rows.Additional Tags: Data, Transparency, Coordination, Organization, In-House Development
rows.Problem Statement: Congress's data task force exists only as a temporary body
rows.Problem Description: The Bulk Data Task Force coordinates how congressional data is structured and released, but it operates without a permanent charter, so its work depends on continued informal support rather than a standing mandate. Data standards work can stall whenever the task force's temporary footing lapses.
rows.Solution Statement: Make the Bulk Data Task Force permanent as the Congressional Data Task Force
rows.Solution Description: Convert the task force into a permanent body, renamed the Congressional Data Task Force, with a standing mandate to coordinate legislative data standards and releases across chambers and support agencies. The rename signals a broader, ongoing mandate rather than a temporary bulk-data project.
rows.Horizon Justification: A permanent charter gives the task force standing authority that survives staff turnover and does not require renewal, so its coordination role becomes a fixed part of the institution.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 47 (tracker Rec 96): Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: In June 2022, CHA directed the Clerk to make the name change in light of its increased scope, and regular meetings have continued.
rows.Concerns: Making the mandate permanent still needs sign-off from both chambers, since the task force coordinates data standards across House and Senate, and bicameral standing-body proposals have stalled before over exactly this kind of shared governance question.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 47

rows.Problem Statement: Members have no required emergency preparedness training
rows.Problem Description: Members face no requirement to train for a crisis that disrupts normal government operations, from a security incident to a mass casualty event at the Capitol. Individual offices and leadership plan informally, but Members themselves are not trained on what to do or where authority sits during an emergency.
rows.Solution Statement: Require emergency preparedness training for Members
rows.Solution Description: Require every Member to complete emergency preparedness training covering what to do and who has authority during a crisis affecting the Capitol or the government's ability to function. Training runs on a recurring schedule tied to House orientation and refresher cycles.
rows.Horizon Justification: Training raises individual readiness but does not itself fix the structural gaps in how Congress continues to operate if Members cannot reach the Capitol, so the underlying continuity problem remains.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 49 (tracker Rec 35): Open-Needs Attention. 118th Congress: Needs a change in House Rules to institute a new requirement. The House currently provides training and tools to offices on request.
rows.Concerns: Training raises individual readiness but leaves the structural continuity-of-government gap untouched: if Members cannot physically reach the Capitol, the same authority and quorum questions the training walks through would still need to be resolved live.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 49

https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/monitoring-the-implementation-of-congressional-modernization-recommendations/

rows.Problem Statement: The House and Senate purchase separately with no shared savings strategy
rows.Problem Description: The House and Senate run separate purchasing processes for overlapping goods and services, from office supplies to equipment, without a shared strategy for combining volume or comparing prices across chambers. Each chamber negotiates alone, so neither captures the savings a joint approach could produce.
rows.Solution Statement: Identify joint purchasing opportunities across chambers
rows.Solution Description: Direct the CAO and Senate Sergeant at Arms to identify specific purchases the House and Senate could combine or streamline to save money, and report findings for further action. The recommendation surfaces opportunities rather than creating a standing joint purchasing function.
rows.Horizon Justification: The recommendation is a one-time review of where savings exist; it does not create an ongoing joint procurement mechanism that would keep capturing those savings automatically.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 50 (tracker Rec 36): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: House and Senate recently coordinated negotiations with a common infrastructure vendor, which could yield savings for both chambers; the CIOs meet regularly.
rows.Concerns: A report identifying savings creates no obligation to act on them, and because the House and Senate run separate appropriations and procurement chains, any joint purchasing still needs both chambers to agree on a shared mechanism.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 50

rows.Problem Statement: House offices purchase goods and services independently at higher cost
rows.Problem Description: Each House office negotiates and buys its own supplies, equipment, and services rather than pooling demand across the chamber. The volume that would justify better pricing and terms is never aggregated, so offices pay more and duplicate the same purchasing work hundreds of times over.
rows.Solution Statement: House-wide bulk purchasing of goods and services
rows.Solution Description: Encourage offices to buy common goods and services through pooled, House-wide contracts instead of negotiating separately. Aggregating demand lowers unit costs and cuts the administrative time each office spends on routine procurement.
rows.Horizon Justification: The recommendation encourages voluntary participation in bulk contracts rather than requiring a centralized purchasing authority, so offices that opt out keep buying independently.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 52 (tracker Rec 37): Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: Report language in the FY2023 Legislative Branch Appropriations Act. Most equipment is bulk-purchased and further progress has been made through the tech store.
rows.Concerns: Participation is voluntary, so offices with an existing preferred vendor or a specific need have no reason to join a pooled contract, and the savings depend on adoption that nothing here requires.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 52

rows.Problem Statement: Rules on member office communications are scattered across many sources
rows.Problem Description: Regulations governing how Member offices communicate, including newsletters, websites, and digital and social media, are issued piecemeal by different House entities over time. Staff must track down guidance from multiple committees and manuals to confirm what is currently allowed, and the rules are hard to locate in one authoritative place.
rows.Solution Statement: Consolidate member communications regulations in one place
rows.Solution Description: Gather the rules governing Member office communications, including digital communications, into a single, easy to find reference. Staff check one source instead of searching across multiple committee guidance documents and manuals.
rows.Horizon Justification: This reorganizes and republishes existing rules rather than changing who sets them or how, so the underlying process for issuing communications guidance stays the same.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 53 (tracker Rec 39): Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: A revised, consolidated Communications Standards Manual was created in 2020 and updated in 2025.
rows.Concerns: Consolidating the rules into one reference does not change who issues them; the same committees keep amending guidance piecemeal afterward, so the single source needs a designated owner or it drifts out of date again.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 53

rows.Problem Statement: The Franking Commission's name no longer matches its role
rows.Problem Description: The House Commission on Mailing Standards, known as the Franking Commission, oversees the full range of Member office communications, not just mail. Its name still reflects a mail-era mandate, so staff and Members do not immediately associate it with the digital communications it also regulates.
rows.Solution Statement: Rename the Franking Commission the House Communications Standards Commission
rows.Solution Description: Rename the House Commission on Mailing Standards the House Communications Standards Commission. The new name signals that the commission's authority covers digital and social media communications alongside mail.
rows.Horizon Justification: A name change clarifies scope but does not alter the commission's authority, staffing, or process, so it leaves the underlying oversight structure unchanged.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 54 (tracker Rec 40): Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 adopted the name change for the Communications Standards Commission, and new branding has been incorporated.
rows.Concerns: The rename touches only the commission's name, leaving its authority, staffing, and process exactly as they are, so any actual gap in how it oversees digital communications continues under a clearer label.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 54

rows.Problem Statement: Constituents have limited channels to reach their Representative
rows.Problem Description: Many offices rely on a narrow set of long-standing contact methods, such as phone lines and mail, and constituents who prefer other channels have fewer ways to reach their Representative. Offices vary widely in what they offer, so the opportunity to communicate depends on which district a constituent lives in.
rows.Solution Statement: Increase constituent communication channels
rows.Solution Description: Direct offices to expand the ways constituents can reach their Representative, adding channels beyond traditional phone and mail. More constituents find a channel that fits how they communicate.
rows.Horizon Justification: The recommendation asks offices to add channels without setting a standard set of channels or a body that maintains them, so adoption and follow-through vary by office.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 55 (tracker Rec 41): Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: The updated Communications Standards Manual allows constituents to subscribe to all forms of member communications, with notice requirements.
rows.Concerns: Directing offices to add channels without naming which ones or assigning anyone to maintain them leaves adoption up to each office's own initiative, reproducing the same district-by-district gap in access the problem describes.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 55

rows.Problem Statement: House social media rules restrict how Members engage followers online
rows.Problem Description: Existing House rules on social media were written before current platform features and formats became standard, so some ordinary interactions between Members and followers fall into ambiguous or restricted territory. Members and staff work around unclear rules rather than using platforms as their audiences expect.
rows.Solution Statement: Update House social media rules
rows.Solution Description: Revise the House rules governing social media use to permit routine, modern forms of engagement between Members and their followers. Members and staff can use current platform features without checking whether an interaction falls outside outdated guidance.
rows.Horizon Justification: The update changes what is permitted under current rules but does not create a standing body to keep those rules current as platforms change, so the same gap can reopen.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 58 (tracker Rec 44): Closed-Implemented. 119th Congress: Throughout 2024-25 the Subcommittee, the Communications Standards Commission, and House Ethics engaged on a proposal to update social media guidelines.
rows.Concerns: Updating the rules once does not create a standing body to revise them as platforms change, so the same ambiguity between what a rule permits and what a platform now does can reopen within a few product cycles.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 58

rows.Problem Statement: Many House offices lack a documented continuity of operations plan
rows.Problem Description: Offices vary in whether they have written plans for safety minimums, emergency communications, and how staff keep working for constituents during a disruption. Without a shared plan available to all staff, continuity depends on what an individual office happened to prepare in advance.
rows.Solution Statement: Require a continuity of operations plan per office
rows.Solution Description: Have each office adopt a continuity of operations plan, including minimum safety requirements and an emergency communications plan, and make it available to all staff. Offices keep serving constituents through a disruption because staff already know the plan.
rows.Horizon Justification: Each office writes and keeps its own plan with no shared owner or enforcement, so plan quality and follow-through still depend on the individual office.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 60 (tracker Rec 46): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The House Sergeant at Arms created a COOP Plan Development Guide for the 117th Congress, available on HouseNet; member offices are not required by rule to adopt one.
rows.Concerns: Each office writes and keeps its own plan with no shared template, owner, or enforcement, so plan quality and follow-through still depend on whether that office's leadership happened to prioritize it, the same variation as today.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 60

rows.Problem Statement: Staff technology and equipment lag behind what remote work requires
rows.Problem Description: Offices differ in how current their laptops, phones, and remote access tools are, and equipment purchases happen on each office's own budget and timeline. When a disruption forces staff to work remotely, offices with older equipment struggle to keep serving constituents at the same level.
rows.Solution Statement: Ensure staff have up-to-date technology and equipment
rows.Solution Description: Provide staff with current technology and equipment so they can keep working effectively on behalf of constituents during a disruption or emergency. Offices spend less time troubleshooting outdated hardware during a crisis.
rows.Horizon Justification: This funds a one-time or periodic equipment refresh rather than a standing mechanism that keeps every office's technology current going forward.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 61 (tracker Rec 47): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The CAO uses bulk purchasing of technology for incoming members; COOP plans and contingencies still need to be incorporated.
rows.Concerns: This funds a one-time equipment refresh rather than a standing replacement cycle, so offices drift back toward uneven, aging hardware within a few years, right up to the next disruption that exposes the gap again.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 61

rows.Problem Statement: Office technology has no routine maintenance schedule
rows.Problem Description: Equipment needed for remote operations and telework is serviced only when something breaks, not on a set schedule. When a remote period arrives, offices discover failures in equipment that regular maintenance would have caught earlier.
rows.Solution Statement: Establish regular maintenance plans for office technology
rows.Solution Description: Set up regular maintenance schedules for office technology so equipment stays functional heading into a remote operations or telework period. Fewer equipment failures surface during the periods when staff depend on it most.
rows.Horizon Justification: This creates a maintenance schedule within each office rather than a standing function or owner responsible for keeping equipment current across the House.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 62 (tracker Rec 48): Closed-Not Implemented. 117th Congress: Existing support offices are not equipped to develop tech maintenance plans for all House offices, though individual offices can do so.
rows.Concerns: Each office sets its own schedule with no House-wide owner or budget line, so offices without IT staff or spare funds skip it just as they do now, leaving the same equipment failures at the offices least equipped to catch them.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 62

rows.Problem Statement: Offices lack shared guidance for constituent communication during a crisis
rows.Problem Description: When a disruption forces extended telework, offices improvise their own outreach plans for staying in touch with constituents rather than drawing on shared guidelines. Constituents get inconsistent information about office availability and services depending on which office they contact.
rows.Solution Statement: Approve and share crisis communications guidelines
rows.Solution Description: Approve crisis communications guidelines for constituent communication, including outreach plans for extended telework periods, and share them with every Member office. Offices have a common starting point for how to reach constituents during a disruption.
rows.Horizon Justification: The guidelines are advisory once shared, and no standing body updates or enforces them, so use and quality still depend on each office.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 63 (tracker Rec 49): Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: The Communications Standards Commission took steps to improve dissemination of mass notices and expedite certain communications without Commission approval.
rows.Concerns: Guidelines are advisory with no enforcement or update mechanism, so offices that already communicate well adopt them and offices that improvise worst keep improvising, leaving the inconsistency the reform names.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 63

rows.Problem Statement: Committees lack bipartisan telework policies
rows.Problem Description: Individual committees set telework arrangements for their staff without a shared, bipartisan process, so policies vary by committee and can shift with a change in chairmanship. Majority and minority staff on the same committee can end up working under different expectations.
rows.Solution Statement: Committees establish bipartisan telework policies
rows.Solution Description: Have each committee set its telework policy on a bipartisan basis, agreed to by both majority and minority staff. Telework expectations hold steady for committee staff regardless of which party controls the gavel.
rows.Horizon Justification: Each committee still sets its own policy independently, so there is no shared standard or owner ensuring consistency across committees or over time.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 66 (tracker Rec 52): Closed-Not Implemented. 118th Congress: Committees may do this now if they choose. Committees' specific operational policies are outside the Subcommittee's purview.
rows.Concerns: Bipartisan sign-off hands minority staff a veto that majority staff, who set telework terms today, have little incentive to grant, and each committee negotiates from scratch, so consistency across chairmanships still depends on every committee choosing it anew.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 66

rows.Problem Statement: Electronic submission of committee reports is a temporary allowance
rows.Problem Description: Committees can submit their reports electronically only under a temporary rule adopted during a period of disrupted operations. Once that rule expires, committees would revert to the paper-based submission process that predates it.
rows.Solution Statement: Make electronic committee report submission permanent
rows.Solution Description: Amend House rules to permanently allow committees to submit reports electronically rather than treating it as a temporary accommodation. Committees file reports electronically as the standing process, not as an exception that needs periodic renewal.
rows.Horizon Justification: This locks a digital process into standing House rules, so it persists on its own without a temporary authorization that must be renewed.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 67 (tracker Rec 53): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: A provision for electronic committee report submission was included in the rules package for the 117th Congress.
rows.Concerns: The change needs floor action on a House rules amendment for a process with modest stakes, so it competes for scarce floor time against reforms with larger payoffs and can end up bundled into a broader rules package as a bargaining chip.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 67

rows.Problem Statement: Most House business still requires physical signatures
rows.Problem Description: Constituent communications and other House business rely on physical or wet signatures for a majority of transactions, requiring staff and Members to be in person or route paper for a signature. This slows routine business and complicates operations whenever staff are not all in the same location.
rows.Solution Statement: Expand digital signatures across House business
rows.Solution Description: Authorize digital signatures for a majority of House business, including constituent communications, replacing the default reliance on physical signatures. Staff complete routine business and constituent responses without waiting on a physical signature.
rows.Horizon Justification: This changes the standing rule for how House business is executed, so digital signatures remain the default going forward without needing repeated approval.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 68 (tracker Rec 54): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: Digital signatures are accepted on all House documents except member travel reports.
rows.Concerns: Expanding digital signatures raises authentication and fraud questions that physical signatures do not, and securing the verification systems needed to catch a forged submission requires investment the rule change itself does not fund.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 68

rows.Problem Statement: Committees have no shared plan for incorporating new technology
rows.Problem Description: Committees adopt new platforms and technology in their daily work in an ad hoc way, without a bipartisan plan agreed to by majority and minority staff. What a committee tries and keeps depends on individual staff interest rather than a deliberate, shared strategy.
rows.Solution Statement: Committees develop bipartisan technology adoption plans
rows.Solution Description: Have each committee develop a bipartisan plan for how technology and innovative platforms can be incorporated into its daily work. Majority and minority staff agree in advance on what gets tried and adopted rather than deciding case by case.
rows.Horizon Justification: Each committee plans independently with no shared infrastructure or owner across committees, so adoption still varies committee by committee.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 69 (tracker Rec 55): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: Several committees have made use of electronic voting; HASC used electronic voting to process amendment votes for the NDAA for the first time.
rows.Concerns: Each committee's plan is independent with no shared infrastructure or House-wide owner, so a chair with little interest in new tools can file a token plan that changes nothing, and adoption still tracks individual chairmanships rather than a durable standard.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 69

rows.Problem Statement: Rules changes are tested nowhere before full adoption
rows.Problem Description: Committees vary widely in their rules and practices, but no institutional practice exists for testing a change at the subcommittee level before applying it committee-wide. Subcommittees that develop a workable idea, on scheduling, markup practice, or staffing, have no defined way to demonstrate it, so committees adopt rules changes outright rather than piloting them first.
rows.Solution Statement: Encourage subcommittee pilots of rules changes
rows.Solution Description: Full committees invite subcommittees to try rules changes on a limited basis and report back on what worked. Committees can then move a successful pilot to full adoption, giving them a low-risk way to test procedural changes before committing the whole committee to them.
rows.Horizon Justification: The idea depends on committee chairs choosing to encourage piloting, with no requirement that any committee adopt the practice, so the existing top-down rules process stays intact.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 76 (tracker Rec 76): Closed-Not Implemented. 118th Congress: Piloted by the Select Committee. The Subcommittee lacks authority to implement the recommendation.
rows.Concerns: The full committee chair controls whether a pilot happens at all, so the reform's reach depends on chairs willing to cede some agenda control, and a pilot that succeeds still has no guaranteed path to committee-wide adoption.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 76

rows.Problem Statement: Committees rarely see policy effects firsthand in the field
rows.Problem Description: Committee travel budgets and CODEL traditions favor bipartisan foreign delegations focused on diplomacy and oversight of foreign policy, while committees have no comparable practice for visiting states and districts to see how domestic programs work on the ground. Members and staff write policy based on hearings and written testimony rather than direct observation of the communities and agencies a program affects.
rows.Solution Statement: Establish committee-based domestic policy CODELs
rows.Solution Description: Give committees a structured way to organize bipartisan delegations focused on domestic programs within their jurisdiction, visiting agency field offices, grantees, and affected communities. Members and staff bring firsthand observations back into hearings and legislative drafting instead of relying only on testimony.
rows.Horizon Justification: The idea establishes a new travel practice committees can use voluntarily, with no requirement that they do so and no change to how committees are funded or staffed.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 78 (tracker Rec 78): Closed-Not Implemented. 118th Congress: Piloted by the Select Committee. The Subcommittee lacks authority to implement the recommendation.
rows.Concerns: Committees already treat foreign CODELs as the more prestigious travel and no new funding accompanies this idea, so domestic delegations compete for the same limited travel budget and staff time against a well-established habit.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 78

rows.Problem Statement: Floor debate is scripted rather than genuine deliberation
rows.Problem Description: House floor time under current rules runs largely on one-minute speeches and pre-written statements timed to the vote clock, with little direct exchange between members holding different views. Members have few chances to test an argument against real-time rebuttal on the floor itself, so the floor functions more as a recording studio than a deliberative space.
rows.Solution Statement: Pilot weekly Oxford-style floor debates
rows.Solution Description: Schedule a recurring weekly slot for a structured, moderated debate on a specific resolution, with members arguing for and against and a vote or informal tally at the close. The pilot runs on a limited schedule so leadership can assess turnout and value before deciding whether to continue it.
rows.Horizon Justification: The debates run as a time-limited pilot, testing the format without committing the floor calendar or House rules to it permanently.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 79 (tracker Rec 79): Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need to coordinate with Leadership on a special order to pilot this.
rows.Concerns: Leadership controls both the floor slot and the decision to continue the pilot, so its survival rests on leadership's willingness to give up scripted, predictable floor time, which is the same dynamic that produced the current format.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 79

rows.Problem Statement: Members and staff receive no formal debate training
rows.Problem Description: Effective floor debate and deliberation are skills, but neither members nor staff receive structured training in them. New members learn by watching colleagues or by trial and error on the floor, and the staff who prepare talking points and debate strategy do so without formal instruction either.
rows.Solution Statement: Debate and deliberation training for members and staff
rows.Solution Description: Offer voluntary training, through orientation or ongoing professional development, that teaches argumentation, rebuttal, and structured deliberation technique. Members and staff who take part bring stronger floor and committee debate skills back to their offices.
rows.Horizon Justification: Training is optional and adds a skill-building resource without changing floor rules, debate formats, or how debate time is allocated.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 80 (tracker Rec 80): Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: Despite the broad variety of courses offered by CAO, none specifically focus on debate or deliberation.
rows.Concerns: Training is voluntary, so it reaches members and staff already inclined toward debate rather than those most in need of it, and it leaves the underlying floor rules that discourage real-time rebuttal untouched.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 80

rows.Problem Statement: Congress lacks the legal capacity to check regulatory action
rows.Problem Description: Executive branch agencies issue regulations with legal and technical staff far larger than what committees or Legislative Counsel can muster to review them. Congress has no dedicated inventory of what additional regulatory and legal staffing would let it meaningfully review, challenge, or shape agency rulemaking.
rows.Solution Statement: Study legislative branch regulatory and legal staffing needs
rows.Solution Description: Commission a review of what additional regulatory and legal resources, in committees, Legislative Counsel, or a new office, would let Congress engage rulemaking and legal disputes with the executive branch as an equal party. The review produces recommendations rather than new staff on its own.
rows.Horizon Justification: The recommendation calls only for identifying needs, not for creating or funding new staff or an office, leaving the underlying resource gap unaddressed until a later decision.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 81 (tracker Rec 81): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: GAO completed its investigation of options for Enhancing Congressional Oversight of Rulemaking and Establishing an Office of Legal Counsel.
rows.Concerns: The study produces recommendations only, with no staffing or funding attached, so it risks joining previous legislative branch capacity reports that identified the same gap between agency and congressional legal resources without a follow-up appropriation ever closing it.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 81

rows.Problem Statement: The legislative branch is thinly represented in litigation
rows.Problem Description: When executive branch action affects Congress's own authority, subpoena enforcement, appropriations riders, or agency non-compliance, the House and Senate rely on small in-house counsel offices that argue those cases on top of their other duties. Courts weigh the legislative branch's arguments unevenly across cases because no consistent, adequately staffed voice represents Congress's institutional interest.
rows.Solution Statement: Strengthen legislative branch court representation
rows.Solution Description: Direct House and Senate legal counsel offices to build the staffing and litigation strategy needed to appear consistently in cases that bear on congressional authority, rather than responding case by case as disputes arise. Congress's institutional position reaches the courts more often and more consistently.
rows.Horizon Justification: The recommendation sets a direction without specifying new staff, budget, or authority, so the existing patchwork of legal counsel offices and ad hoc litigation decisions remains until a more specific reform follows.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 82 (tracker Rec 82): Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Implementing provisions have passed the House as part of the Congressional Subpoena Compliance and Enforcement Act and the Protect Our Democracy Act; needs bicameral action.
rows.Concerns: Directing counsel offices to build litigation capacity without new staff or budget asks offices already stretched thin to do more with the same resources, so the strategy may amount to a plan on paper rather than more consistent courtroom presence.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 82

rows.Problem Statement: Members rarely see how other districts experience shared problems
rows.Problem Description: Members legislate on issues, such as agriculture, manufacturing, or immigration, that play out very differently across the country, but nothing in official travel funding sends a member to see a colleague's district firsthand. Understanding of other districts comes secondhand, through hearings, staff briefings, or informal conversation rather than direct observation.
rows.Solution Statement: Establish a district exchange travel program
rows.Solution Description: Let members use their Members' Representational Allowance to travel to another member's district, on a reciprocal or hosted basis, to see how a shared policy issue plays out there directly. The program runs through the existing MRA and CAO travel administration, so no new appropriation or agency is required to operate it.
rows.Horizon Justification: The program creates a permanent, institution-administered travel category inside the existing MRA framework, so it operates and renews itself without further authorization.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 83 (tracker Rec 83): Closed-Resolved. 117th Congress: Existing Members' Congressional Handbook rules allow for this with documented justification.
rows.Concerns: The program draws on each office's existing MRA rather than new appropriated funds, so offices in expensive media markets or with tighter budgets already spent on district travel are less likely to take part than offices with travel funds to spare.
rows.Sources:
Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, Final Report, H. Rept. 116-562 (Oct. 2020), Rec. 83

rows.Problem Statement: Local funding priorities bypass congressional appropriators entirely
rows.Problem Description: For roughly a decade, directed spending was barred from the appropriations process, leaving decisions about which local infrastructure and community projects get funded largely to executive branch formulas and agency discretion rather than the members closest to the need. Congress's Article One power to direct specific spending sat unused, and local investments received little public accounting when other channels funded them instead.
rows.Solution Statement: Reinstate congressionally-directed spending with disclosure rules
rows.Solution Description: Allow members to request specific, local community investments inside the annual appropriations bills, paired with public disclosure of each request, its sponsor, and its recipient, along with caps on the total amount and the dollar value per request. Appropriations committees administer the disclosure requirements as a standing part of each year's bills.
rows.Horizon Justification: The program is now a standing, disclosed part of the annual appropriations process that recurs every cycle without further legislation to reauthorize it.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 85 (tracker Rec 85): Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: Beginning with the FY2022 appropriations cycle, the Committee on Appropriations reintroduced earmarks through the Community Project Funding program.
rows.Concerns: Reinstating directed spending revives the lobbying and favor-trading pressures that helped end the last round in 2011, and disclosure rules and cap levels are set by each Congress's own appropriators, so a future Congress can loosen them without further debate.
rows.Sources:

rows.Problem Statement: No annual public reckoning of federal fiscal condition exists
rows.Problem Description: The Comptroller General issues a fiscal health report to the executive branch each year, but Congress has no standing annual event of its own that puts the nation's full fiscal picture, revenue, spending, and long-term obligations, before members and the public together. Fiscal debates instead happen piecemeal, bill by bill, without a shared baseline understanding of the government's financial position.
rows.Solution Statement: Require an annual Fiscal State of the Nation
rows.Solution Description: Mandate a yearly joint session or hearing where the Comptroller General presents the federal government's full fiscal picture directly to Congress and the public. The event recurs automatically each year once established in law or standing rule, giving every Congress the same baseline starting point for budget debates.
rows.Horizon Justification: Once required, the event becomes a permanent recurring fixture of the congressional calendar that does not depend on any single Congress choosing to hold it.

rows.Concerns: The mandate guarantees an annual airing of the fiscal picture but creates no mechanism forcing spending or revenue decisions to follow, so Congress can hear the same warning every year and still take no corresponding action.

rows.Problem Statement: The President's budget request offers Congress little useful structure
rows.Problem Description: The executive branch submits its annual budget request in a format and on a timeline that often arrives late and organized in ways that do not match how congressional appropriators actually build bills. Committees end up reconciling the executive's categories with their own before substantive budget work can start.
rows.Solution Statement: Enhance the executive budget submission process
rows.Solution Description: Work with the Office of Management and Budget to improve the timeliness, format, and level of detail in the President's budget submission so it aligns more closely with how appropriations and budget committees use it. Congress starts its own budget work sooner and with less translation between formats.
rows.Horizon Justification: The idea calls for enhancing an existing executive branch submission through negotiation rather than establishing a new congressional structure, leaving the underlying process owned by the executive branch.

rows.Concerns: Congress has no leverage to compel OMB's cooperation, so any improvement depends on a voluntary negotiation that a future administration can simply abandon, leaving the format gap exactly where it was.

rows.Problem Statement: No evidence base exists on biennial budgeting's effects
rows.Problem Description: Proposals to move Congress to a two-year budget and appropriations cycle recur regularly, but no formal evaluation has tested whether a biennial cycle would reduce the year-end pileups and continuing resolutions that slow congressional work now. Advocates and skeptics both argue from intuition rather than evidence.
rows.Solution Statement: Evaluate the effects of biennial budgeting
rows.Solution Description: Commission a study, run by GAO, CBO, or a bipartisan working group, that examines what a two-year budget and appropriations cycle would do to the timeliness and quality of congressional budget work, drawing on states and other bodies that already budget biennially. The findings determine whether Congress adopts a biennial cycle going forward.
rows.Horizon Justification: The recommendation studies the idea rather than adopting it, so the annual budget cycle stays in place until a decision follows.
rows.Current Status (Optional): BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 90 (tracker Rec 90): Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need a biennial budget requirement through statutory revisions to the Congressional Budget Act.
rows.Concerns: GAO and outside researchers have examined biennial budgeting for decades without changing the annual cycle, since both parties value the extra leverage point a yearly bill creates, so another study risks the same fate as its predecessors.

Congressional pay is set office by office with no underlying structure

Each office sets salaries from its own allowance, so pay for the same job varies widely, there is no automatic adjustment for inflation, and a raise depends on a staffer's chief of staff rather than on a schedule. Junior salaries cannot compete with those offered by agencies and firms, and mid-career staff leave before their expertise matures.
Put congressional staff on a structured pay scale

Move staff onto a GS-style scale with defined bands by role and seniority and automatic cost-of-living adjustments, raising junior salaries meaningfully while leaving offices discretion within each band, so pay becomes a property of the job rather than a negotiation each staffer runs alone. Proposals converge on the scale but differ on mechanism: apply the GS scale to committee staff or to all staff; make the existing link between the House staff pay cap and Executive Schedule Level II automatic rather than requiring a fresh Speaker's Pay Order each Congress; raise or remove the personal office staff cap, unchanged since the late 1970s while average district population rose from 519,235 to 761,169; sever the statutory link between the staff pay cap and Member salary so it can be set independently; and direct the CAO to build an inflation-indexing mechanism applied annually to the office allowance formula.
Automatic adjustment removes the annual political decision that keeps pay flat, so the fix persists through changes in leadership and budget climate rather than eroding between one-time increases.

House set a $45,000 minimum staff salary in 2022; no scale exists in either chamber

The House has no hearing room built for non-panel formats

Build a flexible hearing space and incentivize alternative formats

The room and incentive together give committees an alternative venue and a reason to use it, but they do not change hearing rules or the default format used in every other room, so they function as an added option rather than a shift in how hearings are run generally.

No record tracks how much time members spend voting late

Votes have an allotted time window, but the House does not publish any cumulative accounting of how much time individual members spend voting after it closes. Without a public record, there is no visible pressure on the behavior and no way to see whether it is getting better or worse.
Publish a regular late-voting report

Have the House publish a regular report showing the cumulative time each member has spent voting after the allotted window closes. The report gives the public and leadership a standing record to point to, where none currently exists.

Publishing the report creates visibility but no enforcement mechanism. Members who vote late face no formal consequence, so the underlying behavior can continue unchanged even after the report exists.

Committees rarely study how other legislatures solve the same problems

Committee members build relationships and expertise mostly within their own chamber and party, with few structured opportunities to see how other national legislatures handle similar institutional problems. Existing travel is ad hoc and rarely framed around bipartisan learning.
Run semi-regular bipartisan international CODELs

Have the Committee on House Administration and the Committee on Rules jointly organize semi-regular, bipartisan delegations to study how other legislatures operate. Members return with concrete comparisons and, because the trips are bipartisan, with working relationships across party lines that carry back into committee work.

Participation is voluntary and depends on which members choose to travel, so the trips build relationships without changing how committees are structured or staffed. Nothing requires what members learn abroad to change committee practice at home.

Member travel reimbursement rules do not match standard business practice

House rules governing travel related reimbursement for members were written separately from, and have not kept pace with, the standard business travel practices used across the private sector and the rest of the federal government. Members and their offices navigate a reimbursement process that is stricter or more confusing than the norm elsewhere, and travel expenditures are not tracked or reported in a way that supports accountability and transparency.
Align member travel reimbursement with standard practice and improve transparency

Rewrite House rules on member travel related expense reimbursement to match standard business travel practices used in the private sector and elsewhere in the federal government, and update travel expenditure policies to improve efficiency and strengthen accountability and transparency in how travel funds are tracked and reported. Members and offices follow the same kind of reimbursement process used everywhere else, rather than a House-specific variant.
Once the rule is rewritten it applies going forward without further action or funding, so the change is durable and does not depend on any office choosing to opt in.

Lobbying disclosure filings are scattered and hard to search

Lobbyists file disclosure reports with the Clerk of the House and the Secretary of the Senate, but the two systems are separate, not linked, and use inconsistent formats. Consolidate and standardize public lobbying disclosure data

Merge House and Senate lobbying disclosure filings into one standardized, searchable, machine-readable database linked to the bills and issues lobbyists report working on. The public, press, and Congress can then search who is lobbying on a topic in one place instead of checking two separate systems.
A unified disclosure database is a permanent public record system the institution maintains going forward, not a one-time release.

Members receive no required cybersecurity training

Member offices handle sensitive constituent data, legislative strategy, and internal communications, yet Members themselves face no requirement to learn basic cybersecurity practice. Require every Member to complete cybersecurity training on a set schedule, delivered through the House's existing security and IT training infrastructure. Completion becomes a standing condition of office rather than an optional briefing, so awareness of phishing, credential hygiene, and device security holds across turnover.

Staff technology and equipment lag behind what remote work requires

Offices differ in how current their laptops, phones, and remote access tools are, and equipment purchases happen on each office's own budget and timeline. When a disruption forces staff to work remotely, offices with older equipment struggle to keep serving constituents at the same level.
Ensure staff have up-to-date technology and equipment

Provide staff with current technology and equipment so they can keep working effectively on behalf of constituents during a disruption or emergency. Offices spend less time troubleshooting outdated hardware during a crisis.
This funds a one-time or periodic equipment refresh rather than a standing mechanism that keeps every office's technology current going forward.

BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 61 (tracker Rec 47): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: The CAO uses bulk purchasing of technology for incoming members; COOP plans and contingencies still need to be incorporated.

This funds a one-time equipment refresh rather than a standing replacement cycle, so offices drift back toward uneven, aging hardware within a few years, right up to the next disruption that exposes the gap again.

Office technology has no routine maintenance schedule

Equipment needed for remote operations and telework is serviced only when something breaks, not on a set schedule. When a remote period arrives, offices discover failures in equipment that regular maintenance would have caught earlier.
Establish regular maintenance plans for office technology

Set up regular maintenance schedules for office technology so equipment stays functional heading into a remote operations or telework period. Fewer equipment failures surface during the periods when staff depend on it most.
This creates a maintenance schedule within each office rather than a standing function or owner responsible for keeping equipment current across the House.

BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 62 (tracker Rec 48): Closed-Not Implemented. 117th Congress: Existing support offices are not equipped to develop tech maintenance plans for all House offices, though individual offices can do so.

Offices lack shared guidance for constituent communication during a crisis

When a disruption forces extended telework, offices improvise their own outreach plans for staying in touch with constituents rather than drawing on shared guidelines. Constituents get inconsistent information about office availability and services depending on which office they contact.
Approve and share crisis communications guidelines

Approve crisis communications guidelines for constituent communication, including outreach plans for extended telework periods, and share them with every Member office. Offices have a common starting point for how to reach constituents during a disruption.
The guidelines are advisory once shared, and no standing body updates or enforces them, so use and quality still depend on each office.

BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 63 (tracker Rec 49): Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: The Communications Standards Commission took steps to improve dissemination of mass notices and expedite certain communications without Commission approval.

Guidelines are advisory with no enforcement or update mechanism, so offices that already communicate well adopt them and offices that improvise worst keep improvising, leaving the inconsistency the reform names.

Committees lack bipartisan telework policies

Individual committees set telework arrangements for their staff without a shared, bipartisan process, so policies vary by committee and can shift with a change in chairmanship. Majority and minority staff on the same committee can end up working under different expectations.
Committees establish bipartisan telework policies

Have each committee set its telework policy on a bipartisan basis, agreed to by both majority and minority staff. Telework expectations hold steady for committee staff regardless of which party controls the gavel.
Each committee still sets its own policy independently, so there is no shared standard or owner ensuring consistency across committees or over time.

BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 66 (tracker Rec 52): Closed-Not Implemented. 118th Congress: Committees may do this now if they choose. Committees' specific operational policies are outside the Subcommittee's purview.

Bipartisan sign-off hands minority staff a veto that majority staff, who set telework terms today, have little incentive to grant, and each committee negotiates from scratch, so consistency across chairmanships still depends on every committee choosing it anew.

Electronic submission of committee reports is a temporary allowance

Committees can submit their reports electronically only under a temporary rule adopted during a period of disrupted operations. Once that rule expires, committees would revert to the paper-based submission process that predates it.
Make electronic committee report submission permanent

Amend House rules to permanently allow committees to submit reports electronically rather than treating it as a temporary accommodation. Committees file reports electronically as the standing process, not as an exception that needs periodic renewal.
This locks a digital process into standing House rules, so it persists on its own without a temporary authorization that must be renewed.

BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 67 (tracker Rec 53): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: A provision for electronic committee report submission was included in the rules package for the 117th Congress.

The change needs floor action on a House rules amendment for a process with modest stakes, so it competes for scarce floor time against reforms with larger payoffs and can end up bundled into a broader rules package as a bargaining chip.

Most House business still requires physical signatures

Constituent communications and other House business rely on physical or wet signatures for a majority of transactions, requiring staff and Members to be in person or route paper for a signature. This slows routine business and complicates operations whenever staff are not all in the same location.
Expand digital signatures across House business

Authorize digital signatures for a majority of House business, including constituent communications, replacing the default reliance on physical signatures. Staff complete routine business and constituent responses without waiting on a physical signature.
This changes the standing rule for how House business is executed, so digital signatures remain the default going forward without needing repeated approval.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 68 (tracker Rec 54): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: Digital signatures are accepted on all House documents except member travel reports.

Expanding digital signatures raises authentication and fraud questions that physical signatures do not, and securing the verification systems needed to catch a forged submission requires investment the rule change itself does not fund.

Committees have no shared plan for incorporating new technology

Committees adopt new platforms and technology in their daily work in an ad hoc way, without a bipartisan plan agreed to by majority and minority staff. What a committee tries and keeps depends on individual staff interest rather than a deliberate, shared strategy.
Committees develop bipartisan technology adoption plans

Have each committee develop a bipartisan plan for how technology and innovative platforms can be incorporated into its daily work. Majority and minority staff agree in advance on what gets tried and adopted rather than deciding case by case.
Each committee plans independently with no shared infrastructure or owner across committees, so adoption still varies committee by committee.

BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 69 (tracker Rec 55): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: Several committees have made use of electronic voting; HASC used electronic voting to process amendment votes for the NDAA for the first time.

Each committee's plan is independent with no shared infrastructure or House-wide owner, so a chair with little interest in new tools can file a token plan that changes nothing, and adoption still tracks individual chairmanships rather than a durable standard.

Rules changes are tested nowhere before full adoption

Committees vary widely in their rules and practices, but no institutional practice exists for testing a change at the subcommittee level before applying it committee-wide. Subcommittees that develop a workable idea, on scheduling, markup practice, or staffing, have no defined way to demonstrate it, so committees adopt rules changes outright rather than piloting them first.
Encourage subcommittee pilots of rules changes

Full committees invite subcommittees to try rules changes on a limited basis and report back on what worked. Committees can then move a successful pilot to full adoption, giving them a low-risk way to test procedural changes before committing the whole committee to them.
The idea depends on committee chairs choosing to encourage piloting, with no requirement that any committee adopt the practice, so the existing top-down rules process stays intact.

BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 76 (tracker Rec 76): Closed-Not Implemented. 118th Congress: Piloted by the Select Committee. The Subcommittee lacks authority to implement the recommendation.

The full committee chair controls whether a pilot happens at all, so the reform's reach depends on chairs willing to cede some agenda control, and a pilot that succeeds still has no guaranteed path to committee-wide adoption.

Committees rarely see policy effects firsthand in the field

Committee travel budgets and CODEL traditions favor bipartisan foreign delegations focused on diplomacy and oversight of foreign policy, while committees have no comparable practice for visiting states and districts to see how domestic programs work on the ground. Members and staff write policy based on hearings and written testimony rather than direct observation of the communities and agencies a program affects.
Establish committee-based domestic policy CODELs

Give committees a structured way to organize bipartisan delegations focused on domestic programs within their jurisdiction, visiting agency field offices, grantees, and affected communities. Members and staff bring firsthand observations back into hearings and legislative drafting instead of relying only on testimony.
The idea establishes a new travel practice committees can use voluntarily, with no requirement that they do so and no change to how committees are funded or staffed.

BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 78 (tracker Rec 78): Closed-Not Implemented. 118th Congress: Piloted by the Select Committee. The Subcommittee lacks authority to implement the recommendation.

Committees already treat foreign CODELs as the more prestigious travel and no new funding accompanies this idea, so domestic delegations compete for the same limited travel budget and staff time against a well-established habit.

Floor debate is scripted rather than genuine deliberation

House floor time under current rules runs largely on one-minute speeches and pre-written statements timed to the vote clock, with little direct exchange between members holding different views. Members have few chances to test an argument against real-time rebuttal on the floor itself, so the floor functions more as a recording studio than a deliberative space.
Pilot weekly Oxford-style floor debates

Schedule a recurring weekly slot for a structured, moderated debate on a specific resolution, with members arguing for and against and a vote or informal tally at the close. The pilot runs on a limited schedule so leadership can assess turnout and value before deciding whether to continue it.
The debates run as a time-limited pilot, testing the format without committing the floor calendar or House rules to it permanently.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 79 (tracker Rec 79): Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need to coordinate with Leadership on a special order to pilot this.

Leadership controls both the floor slot and the decision to continue the pilot, so its survival rests on leadership's willingness to give up scripted, predictable floor time, which is the same dynamic that produced the current format.

Members and staff receive no formal debate training

Effective floor debate and deliberation are skills, but neither members nor staff receive structured training in them. New members learn by watching colleagues or by trial and error on the floor, and the staff who prepare talking points and debate strategy do so without formal instruction either.
Debate and deliberation training for members and staff

Offer voluntary training, through orientation or ongoing professional development, that teaches argumentation, rebuttal, and structured deliberation technique. Members and staff who take part bring stronger floor and committee debate skills back to their offices.
Training is optional and adds a skill-building resource without changing floor rules, debate formats, or how debate time is allocated.

BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 80 (tracker Rec 80): Open-In Progress. 118th Congress: Despite the broad variety of courses offered by CAO, none specifically focus on debate or deliberation.

Training is voluntary, so it reaches members and staff already inclined toward debate rather than those most in need of it, and it leaves the underlying floor rules that discourage real-time rebuttal untouched.

Congress lacks the legal capacity to check regulatory action

Executive branch agencies issue regulations with legal and technical staff far larger than what committees or Legislative Counsel can muster to review them. Congress has no dedicated inventory of what additional regulatory and legal staffing would let it meaningfully review, challenge, or shape agency rulemaking.
Study legislative branch regulatory and legal staffing needs

Commission a review of what additional regulatory and legal resources, in committees, Legislative Counsel, or a new office, would let Congress engage rulemaking and legal disputes with the executive branch as an equal party. The review produces recommendations rather than new staff on its own.
The recommendation calls only for identifying needs, not for creating or funding new staff or an office, leaving the underlying resource gap unaddressed until a later decision.

BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 81 (tracker Rec 81): Closed-Implemented. 118th Congress: GAO completed its investigation of options for Enhancing Congressional Oversight of Rulemaking and Establishing an Office of Legal Counsel.

The study produces recommendations only, with no staffing or funding attached, so it risks joining previous legislative branch capacity reports that identified the same gap between agency and congressional legal resources without a follow-up appropriation ever closing it.

The legislative branch is thinly represented in litigation

When executive branch action affects Congress's own authority, subpoena enforcement, appropriations riders, or agency non-compliance, the House and Senate rely on small in-house counsel offices that argue those cases on top of their other duties. Courts weigh the legislative branch's arguments unevenly across cases because no consistent, adequately staffed voice represents Congress's institutional interest.
Strengthen legislative branch court representation

Direct House and Senate legal counsel offices to build the staffing and litigation strategy needed to appear consistently in cases that bear on congressional authority, rather than responding case by case as disputes arise. Congress's institutional position reaches the courts more often and more consistently.

The recommendation sets a direction without specifying new staff, budget, or authority, so the existing patchwork of legal counsel offices and ad hoc litigation decisions remains until a more specific reform follows.

BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 82 (tracker Rec 82): Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Implementing provisions have passed the House as part of the Congressional Subpoena Compliance and Enforcement Act and the Protect Our Democracy Act; needs bicameral action.

Directing counsel offices to build litigation capacity without new staff or budget asks offices already stretched thin to do more with the same resources, so the strategy may amount to a plan on paper rather than more consistent courtroom presence.

Members rarely see how other districts experience shared problems

Members legislate on issues, such as agriculture, manufacturing, or immigration, that play out very differently across the country, but nothing in official travel funding sends a member to see a colleague's district firsthand. Understanding of other districts comes secondhand, through hearings, staff briefings, or informal conversation rather than direct observation.
Establish a district exchange travel program

Let members use their Members' Representational Allowance to travel to another member's district, on a reciprocal or hosted basis, to see how a shared policy issue plays out there directly. The program runs through the existing MRA and CAO travel administration, so no new appropriation or agency is required to operate it.
The program creates a permanent, institution-administered travel category inside the existing MRA framework, so it operates and renews itself without further authorization.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 83 (tracker Rec 83): Closed-Resolved. 117th Congress: Existing Members' Congressional Handbook rules allow for this with documented justification.

The program draws on each office's existing MRA rather than new appropriated funds, so offices in expensive media markets or with tighter budgets already spent on district travel are less likely to take part than offices with travel funds to spare.
