Local funding priorities bypass congressional appropriators entirely

For roughly a decade, directed spending was barred from the appropriations process, leaving decisions about which local infrastructure and community projects get funded largely to executive branch formulas and agency discretion rather than the members closest to the need. Congress's Article One power to direct specific spending sat unused, and local investments received little public accounting when other channels funded them instead.
Reinstate congressionally-directed spending with disclosure rules

Allow members to request specific, local community investments inside the annual appropriations bills, paired with public disclosure of each request, its sponsor, and its recipient, along with caps on the total amount and the dollar value per request. Appropriations committees administer the disclosure requirements as a standing part of each year's bills.
The program is now a standing, disclosed part of the annual appropriations process that recurs every cycle without further legislation to reauthorize it.

BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 85 (tracker Rec 85): Closed-Implemented. 117th Congress: Beginning with the FY2022 appropriations cycle, the Committee on Appropriations reintroduced earmarks through the Community Project Funding program.

Reinstating directed spending revives the lobbying and favor-trading pressures that helped end the last round in 2011, and disclosure rules and cap levels are set by each Congress's own appropriators, so a future Congress can loosen them without further debate.

No annual public reckoning of federal fiscal condition exists

The Comptroller General issues a fiscal health report to the executive branch each year, but Congress has no standing annual event of its own that puts the nation's full fiscal picture, revenue, spending, and long-term obligations, before members and the public together. Fiscal debates instead happen piecemeal, bill by bill, without a shared baseline understanding of the government's financial position.
Require an annual Fiscal State of the Nation

Mandate a yearly joint session or hearing where the Comptroller General presents the federal government's full fiscal picture directly to Congress and the public. The event recurs automatically each year once established in law or standing rule, giving every Congress the same baseline starting point for budget debates.
Once required, the event becomes a permanent recurring fixture of the congressional calendar that does not depend on any single Congress choosing to hold it.

The mandate guarantees an annual airing of the fiscal picture but creates no mechanism forcing spending or revenue decisions to follow, so Congress can hear the same warning every year and still take no corresponding action.

The President's budget request offers Congress little useful structure

The executive branch submits its annual budget request in a format and on a timeline that often arrives late and organized in ways that do not match how congressional appropriators actually build bills. Committees end up reconciling the executive's categories with their own before substantive budget work can start.
Enhance the executive budget submission process

Work with the Office of Management and Budget to improve the timeliness, format, and level of detail in the President's budget submission so it aligns more closely with how appropriations and budget committees use it. Congress starts its own budget work sooner and with less translation between formats.

The idea calls for enhancing an existing executive branch submission through negotiation rather than establishing a new congressional structure, leaving the underlying process owned by the executive branch.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 89 (tracker Rec 89): Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need statutory revisions to the Congressional Budget Act.

Congress has no leverage to compel OMB's cooperation, so any improvement depends on a voluntary negotiation that a future administration can simply abandon, leaving the format gap exactly where it was.

No evidence base exists on biennial budgeting's effects

Proposals to move Congress to a two-year budget and appropriations cycle recur regularly, but no formal evaluation has tested whether a biennial cycle would reduce the year-end pileups and continuing resolutions that slow congressional work now. Advocates and skeptics both argue from intuition rather than evidence.
Evaluate the effects of biennial budgeting

Commission a study, run by GAO, CBO, or a bipartisan working group, that examines what a two-year budget and appropriations cycle would do to the timeliness and quality of congressional budget work, drawing on states and other bodies that already budget biennially. The findings determine whether Congress adopts a biennial cycle going forward.
The recommendation studies the idea rather than adopting it, so the annual budget cycle stays in place until a decision follows.
BPC tracker (Apr 2026), H. Rept. 116-562 Rec 90 (tracker Rec 90): Open-Needs Attention. 117th Congress: Need a biennial budget requirement through statutory revisions to the Congressional Budget Act.

GAO and outside researchers have examined biennial budgeting for decades without changing the annual cycle, since both parties value the extra leverage point a yearly bill creates, so another study risks the same fate as its predecessors.
